# OpenAI in Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode

OpenAI serves its models on two APIs at `api.openai.com`: Responses and Chat Completions. Its own models are best asked on Responses, and its newest answer only there. Add an OpenAI API key to jianmu once, and Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and every other agent you connect can use OpenAI’s models through jianmu’s local gateway at `127.0.0.1:3425`, each agent with a model of its own. Codex’s requests go to OpenAI as they are; the other agents’ are translated on the way.

This page is about an API key from platform.openai.com. A ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription is signed in to separately; see [Subscriptions in any agent](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/subscriptions).

## Add OpenAI

1. **Get a key.** Make one on [platform.openai.com](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys). It starts with `sk-`.
2. **Add the provider.** In jianmu’s Providers tab, press ＋ Add provider, pick OpenAI, paste the key and save. jianmu asks OpenAI which models the key can use.
3. **Pick it for an agent.** In the Agents tab, click the model on the agent’s row and choose an OpenAI model such as `gpt-6.1-sol`.

```
jianmu provider add openai <key>
jianmu provider test openai
```

Model ids in jianmu are `provider/model`, so OpenAI’s read `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`: the provider, then OpenAI’s own id. The key is kept in jianmu’s settings; jianmu doesn’t take it from your shell.

Already set OpenAI up in OpenCode or another app jianmu imports from? The import brings it in as the OpenAI provider.

## Endpoints

| API | Address | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Responses | `https://api.openai.com/v1` | OpenAI’s own models, ids starting `gpt-`, `codex` or `o` and a digit: Codex’s requests as they are, Claude Code’s, Gemini CLI’s and OpenCode’s translated |
| Chat Completions | `https://api.openai.com/v1` | the model list, and any other model the key lists |

jianmu’s OpenAI provider has no Anthropic Messages address, so Claude Code’s requests are always translated. For OpenAI’s own models jianmu keeps Responses first even for an agent that speaks Chat Completions. When OpenAI answers that a model is served only on `/v1/responses`, jianmu asks again there and remembers it. To send a model on one API yourself:

```
jianmu model api openai/gpt-5.5 chat
jianmu model api openai/gpt-5.5 --reset
jianmu model apis openai
```

**Azure OpenAI** is a provider of its own, Azure OpenAI. Give it your resource’s endpoint, `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`, and its key. jianmu uses the v1 API under `/openai/v1` for Chat Completions and Responses, sends the key in the `api-key` header, and lists the resource’s deployments as its models. A deployment named for its model, such as `gpt-5-codex`, goes to Responses first too.

## Model list

jianmu fetches the list from OpenAI, at `https://api.openai.com/v1/models`, so agents see the models your key can use. Names, context windows, reasoning levels and prices come from models.dev’s `openai` catalog. A reasoning model OpenAI has just listed, before its levels are known, gets those of the newest reasoning model in its family: `gpt-6.1-sol` got `gpt-6-sol`’s. Pick the models agents see in the provider’s model list, or from the terminal:

```
jianmu provider models openai +gpt-6.1-sol +gpt-6-luna +gpt-5.5
jianmu provider refresh-every openai 1d
```

## In each agent

```
jianmu claude openai/gpt-6.1-sol
jianmu codex openai/gpt-6.1-sol
jianmu gemini model openai/gpt-6.1-sol
jianmu opencode openai/gpt-6.1-sol
```

- **Claude Code.** speaks Anthropic Messages, which OpenAI doesn’t serve. jianmu translates each request to Responses and the reply back; the model’s reasoning summary reaches Claude Code as thinking, then the text. [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models).
- **Codex.** speaks Responses, so its requests go to OpenAI as they are: its custom tools such as `apply_patch`, its reasoning items and its own `prompt_cache_key` included. Codex is also offered Fast here; see Reasoning. [Models in Codex](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/codex-models).
- **Gemini CLI.** speaks Google’s Gemini API. jianmu translates each request to Responses and the reply back. [Models in Gemini CLI](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/gemini-cli-models).
- **OpenCode.** speaks Chat Completions. OpenAI’s own models go to Responses first, so jianmu translates its requests there and the replies back; any other model the key lists gets OpenCode’s requests as they are. [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models).

## What jianmu does for OpenAI

- **A prompt cache key..** A translated request to OpenAI that carries no `prompt_cache_key` gets one, made from the session the agent names, or else its first user message, and hashed, so it names nothing of the agent. Codex sends its own, which goes on as it is, and one you set yourself wins. If OpenAI answers 400 over the field, jianmu asks again without it.
- **Tools loaded where they were loaded..** A tool that Claude Code’s tool search loads mid-conversation is sent to OpenAI’s Responses API as an `additional_tools` item at that point, not added to the tool list, which keeps the cached prefix. `additional-tools=off` puts it with the other tools.
- **Sealed reasoning from elsewhere..** OpenAI reads only its own sealed reasoning (`encrypted_content`). An item sealed under another key, organization or account is refused (“could not be verified”); jianmu asks again without those items and remembers it for the conversation. Claude’s thinking, which Codex carries in a reasoning item after a turn on a Claude model, is taken out before the request reaches OpenAI.
- **Earlier responses..** A Responses client may send only a turn’s new input and name the response it follows (`previous_response_id`). jianmu keeps each response it gave such a client, in memory and under the caller’s gateway key. OpenAI keeps responses too, so when the same key answered the one named, OpenAI is sent only the new input after its own id. Codex over HTTP says `store` false and names none.
- **Codex’s own compaction..** With `compaction=native`, Codex’s compaction is asked of OpenAI as Codex sent it and the sealed item comes back to Codex as it came. Only the key that sealed it can read it, so later requests carrying it go only there. The default, `compaction=jianmu`, has jianmu summarise.

```
jianmu provider set openai compaction=native
jianmu provider set openai additional-tools=off
```

## Reasoning

- **Effort..** The effort an agent asks for is fitted to the nearest level the model has, as the catalog lists them: `gpt-6-sol` has `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`. On Responses it is sent as `reasoning.effort`, with `summary` set to `auto`, so the model’s reasoning summary comes back.
- **Reasoning off..** When an agent whose requests jianmu translates, such as Gemini CLI, turns reasoning off and the model lists `none` among its levels, jianmu asks for none.
- **Encrypted reasoning..** jianmu passes on what an agent asks to include, but asks for `reasoning.encrypted_content` only with reasoning: OpenAI refuses it of a model that doesn’t reason. Codex sends the sealed items back on the next turn, and jianmu passes them on as they are.
- **Fast..** On an OpenAI key, Codex is offered Fast for GPT and o-series models. jianmu sends it as `service_tier: "priority"`, OpenAI’s priority processing. A service tier set for Codex in jianmu overrides what Codex asked.

## Web search

OpenAI’s Responses API searches the web itself. When an agent offers its model web search, as Codex and Claude Code do, jianmu gives the model OpenAI’s own `web_search` tool on Responses, and OpenAI runs the search.

## Cost and usage

- **Cost..** The Usage tab prices each call with OpenAI’s prices from models.dev.
- **Cache tokens..** When a reply reports cached prompt tokens, the Usage tab counts them apart from the rest of the prompt.
- **Keeping the cache..** With several keys, a conversation stays on its key while its cache is worth keeping, 1,024 tokens or more, and still warm, read within the last five minutes.
- **Service tier..** Each call records the tier the agent asked for, the one jianmu sent, and the one OpenAI’s reply says it ran at.
- **Balance..** jianmu reads no balance from OpenAI; type it in with `key-balance`, and the Usage page shows it less what jianmu has priced the key’s calls at since.

## Several keys and failover

One OpenAI provider can hold several keys: press Add another key under it, or paste several at once. Requests go to the first key that’s on, and when it runs out or is rate limited the next one takes over. To keep keys apart instead, say from two organizations, add the provider again: the second is `openai-2`.

- **Spend caps..** `spend-cap` stops a key at a dollar amount a day, a month or in all, as the Usage tab prices its calls; routing then goes on to the other keys and the fallbacks.
- **Fallbacks..** `fallback` names where requests go when OpenAI is out of quota or down: another provider’s model or a routing group.

```
jianmu provider spend-cap openai <key> 20 month
jianmu provider key-balance openai <key> 25
jianmu provider fallback openai deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
```

## Troubleshooting

- **“The encrypted content for item rs_… could not be verified”..** The conversation carries reasoning sealed under another key, organization or account. jianmu asks again without those items; see What jianmu does.
- **A model that answers only on `/v1/responses`..** jianmu moves it to Responses and remembers it. `jianmu model apis openai` shows which API each model is asked on.
- **A 400 over `prompt_cache_key`..** jianmu asks again without the key it added.
- **Checking a key..** `jianmu provider test openai` sends a tiny request through each endpoint, or to each model you name. Add `--as codex` or `--as claude-code` to send it the way that agent would.

## FAQ

### How do I use OpenAI’s models in Claude Code?

Add your OpenAI API key in jianmu (Providers, Add provider, OpenAI), then pick a model such as `gpt-6.1-sol` on Claude Code’s row, or run `jianmu claude openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. OpenAI serves no Anthropic Messages API, so jianmu translates Claude Code’s requests to OpenAI’s Responses API at `https://api.openai.com/v1` and the replies back, the reasoning summary as thinking.

### Can Codex use an OpenAI API key instead of a ChatGPT sign-in?

Yes. Add the key, then run `jianmu codex openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. Codex speaks Responses, so its requests go to OpenAI as they are, custom tools and reasoning included, and Fast is sent as priority processing. A ChatGPT Plus or Pro sign-in is set up separately, in Subscriptions.

### How do I use GPT models in OpenCode?

Pick the model in jianmu, or run `jianmu opencode openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. OpenCode speaks Chat Completions, but OpenAI’s own models go to Responses first, so jianmu translates OpenCode’s requests there and the replies back. To send a model on Chat Completions instead, run `jianmu model api openai/gpt-5.5 chat`.

### Can Gemini CLI use OpenAI?

Yes. Gemini CLI speaks Google’s Gemini API, so jianmu translates its requests to OpenAI’s Responses API and the replies back, streaming and tool calls included. Run `jianmu gemini model openai/gpt-6.1-sol`.

### Does jianmu keep OpenAI’s prompt cache?

Yes. Codex’s own `prompt_cache_key` goes on as it is. A translated request without one gets a key made from its session or first user message, hashed so it names nothing of the agent. With several keys, a conversation stays on its key while its cache is warm.

### Why does OpenAI say the encrypted content could not be verified?

OpenAI reads only reasoning it sealed for the same key, organization or account. When a conversation carries reasoning sealed elsewhere, jianmu asks again without those items and remembers it for the conversation.

### Does jianmu support Azure OpenAI?

Yes, as its own provider, Azure OpenAI. Give it the resource’s endpoint and key; jianmu uses the v1 API under `/openai/v1`, sends the key in the `api-key` header and lists the resource’s deployments as models.

**By provider:** [DeepSeek](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/deepseek) · [Kimi and Kimi Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/kimi) · [GLM Coding Plan](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/glm) · [Volcengine Ark](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/volcengine) · [Tencent Cloud](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/tencent-cloud) · [Baidu Qianfan](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/baidu-qianfan) · [SiliconFlow](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/siliconflow) · [ModelScope](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/modelscope) · [Huawei Cloud MaaS](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/huaweicloud) · [Xiaomi MiMo](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/xiaomi-mimo) · [StepFun](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/stepfun) · [LongCat](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/longcat) · [Qwen](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/qwen) · [MiniMax](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/minimax) · [Anthropic](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/anthropic) · [Gemini](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/gemini) · [Grok](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/grok) · [Mistral](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/mistral) · [OpenRouter](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/openrouter) · [GitHub Copilot](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/copilot) · [Ollama](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/ollama)

Every agent: [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models), [Models in Codex](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/codex-models), [Models in Gemini CLI](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/gemini-cli-models), [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models). Ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues) if you get stuck.

# Intent routing

Send a turn to a model by what the user asks for: tests to the strong model, quick questions to the fast cheap one. You describe each kind in a few words. When a turn begins, a small model you choose picks which kind the message is.

Intent is one of the conditions a [routing group’s rule](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/start#rules) can have, next to length, images, reasoning and agent. This page describes exactly what jianmu does with it, as of v0.1.99, so you can predict every decision and check it in the Routing tab.

> **In one paragraph.** jianmu decides once per turn: when you send a message, not while the agent works through tool calls. If a rule with an intent could be the first to match, jianmu asks the group’s *classifier* model one short question through its own gateway. The question holds the intents as a numbered list plus the text of your latest message, and the classifier answers with a number. jianmu reads that number and checks the rules top first with it. The first rule that matches puts its model first, and the group’s other models stay behind it for failover. The turn then stays on that model until you speak again. If the classifier fails, times out or answers something else, no intent matches and the turn is routed as if those rules weren’t there. There are no embeddings, no keyword lists and no training: the model you pick reads your message and picks a number.

## Set it up

You need a [routing group](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/start#routing) with at least two models, and one more model to classify with. The classifier can be any model jianmu has, in the group or not.

1. **Open the group.** Go to Routing, find the group under *Routing groups* and click Edit.
2. **Add a rule with an intent.** Click Add a rule. The new rule reads asks for → a model, with the intent box ready: type what the message asks for, such as *writing or fixing tests*, then pick the model after →. More conditions come from the rule’s +, and must hold too.
3. **Pick the classifier.** Intent told by appears once a rule has an intent, set to Jev when you have a TypeSafe provider. Otherwise choose a small, fast model without reasoning. A group whose effort Jev already picks offers the same under its classifier: It can pick the model too. A group can’t be saved with an intent and no classifier.
4. **Save, and send a message.** Changes apply from the next turn, with no restart. The Routing tab shows what the classifier said and where the turn went.

The timeout is global: in Settings → Models → Replies → Intent classifier timeout, choose 8, 15, 30 or 60 seconds. It defaults to 8 seconds and applies to the next classifier call, including Jev, with no restart. A slow classifier may need longer, but the turn waits for it before routing. In `~/.config/jianmu/settings.json`, `"classifyTimeout"` accepts whole seconds from 1 to 60; 0 or a missing field uses 8. A custom value in that range appears as its own choice in Settings.

The same from a terminal:

```
jianmu group rule add coder use=deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash intent="a quick question" classifier=groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant
jianmu group rule add coder use=deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro intent="writing or fixing tests"
jianmu group rule add coder use=deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro use-effort=low intent="a simple edit"   # the same model, asked for low reasoning
jianmu group rule coder                           # the rules, numbered, and the classifier
jianmu group rule classifier coder groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant   # change the classifier
jianmu group rule mv coder 3 1                    # order matters: top first
jianmu group rule rm coder 2
```

`intent=` also takes the spellings `asks=` and `about=`. `classifier=` also takes `classify=` and `by=`. `classifier=` on `rule add` sets the group’s classifier and is needed only the first time. The classifier is saved in the group’s record in `~/.config/jianmu/providers.json` as `"classifier"`, and each rule as `{"use": …, "intent": …}`.

A rule can also set the reasoning its model is asked for, so an intent picks the model and the effort as a pair: `use-effort=` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`), saved as `"useEffort"`, such as `{"use": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro", "intent": "a simple edit", "useEffort": "low"}`. In the editor it is set from the rule’s ⋯ menu, Set its reasoning, and shows beside the model. The rule’s model is then asked for that effort on the turn’s requests, whatever the agent asked, at the model’s nearest level. A model whose levels jianmu doesn’t know is asked as the agent asked, and so are the models the group fails over to. A model fixed at an effort in the group keeps its own. Without it, the model is asked as the agent asked. The Routing tab says when a rule set the effort.

## How a turn is routed

Every request an agent sends to a group with rules goes through these steps, in this order:

1. **Is this a new turn?.** jianmu looks at the request’s last user message. If it carries text or an image and no tool result, you just spoke, so a new turn begins. If it carries tool results, the agent is continuing a turn already under way (see The rest of the turn). Turns are counted per conversation. A subagent is its own conversation: it shares its agent’s session but starts with different words.
2. **Which intents could decide?.** jianmu walks the rules top first and ignores intent for now: a rule is a candidate if its other conditions (tokens, images, reasoning, agents) hold for this request. Each candidate’s intent is collected, and duplicates spelled the same apart from case count once. The walk stops at the first candidate *without* an intent, because that rule matches outright and nothing below it could come first. If no intents were collected, the classifier isn’t asked and costs nothing.
3. **Ask the classifier.** jianmu sends the classifier the collected intents and the text of your message. The exact prompt is shown below. The call goes through jianmu’s own gateway, like a request from an agent, so it uses that model’s provider with its keys or accounts and their failover. It has the configured timeout to answer (8 seconds by default).
4. **Read the answer.** jianmu takes the first whole number in the reply. `1` to `n` names that intent, and `0` means none of them. Anything else, such as no number or one out of range, counts as a failure. The answer is kept for 10 minutes for the same message and intents.
5. **Match the rules.** The rules are checked top first with the answer. A rule with an intent matches only when the classifier named its intent, compared without case, and all its other conditions hold. The first rule that matches wins. If none matches, the group routes the turn as it always does.
6. **Order the models.** The winning rule’s model goes first, and the group’s other models follow in their usual order as failover. This holds even if another model answered the conversation’s last turn: a rule outranks the Stays setting as a turn begins. If the rule’s model has nothing ready right now (every key resting, the provider off), the group’s usual order stands and the trace says so.
7. **Remember the decision.** jianmu keeps the decision for this conversation (the group, the agent’s session and the conversation’s first words) with the classifier’s answer, so the rest of the turn follows it.

### An example

The Coder group above has three rules:

| # | When | Send to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | ≥ 128000 tokens | kimi/kimi-k2.5 |
| 2 | asks for “a quick question” | deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash |
| 3 | asks for “writing or fixing tests” | deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro |

- A 20k-token turn: rule 1 doesn’t hold, so both intents are candidates. The classifier is asked to choose between “a quick question” and “writing or fixing tests”.
- A 150k-token turn: rule 1 has no intent and holds, so the walk stops there. The classifier isn’t asked, and the turn goes to Kimi.
- The classifier says `0` (none): no rule matches, and the turn goes by the group’s routing (here *In order*, so deepseek-v4-pro first).

### In the app

A real request through a group with two intent rules (“a quick question or explanation, with no code to write or change” and “writing or fixing tests”), sent from Claude Code: “Add unit tests for the LRU cache in cache.go, covering eviction and concurrent reads and writes”. The Routing tab shows it as it happens.

## What the classifier sees

This is the whole request, and nothing else is sent. The system message is fixed. The user message lists your intents in rule order, as they were collected in step 2:

```
You route a user's message to a coding assistant by what it asks for. Given numbered kinds of request and the user's message, answer with the number of the kind the message is, or 0 if it is none of them. Answer with the number only.
```

```
Kinds:
1. a quick question
2. writing or fixing tests

The user's message:
<message>
Write unit tests for the parseTokens function and fix any that fail.
</message>

The number of its kind (0 for none):
```

- **Only your latest message..** jianmu sends the text parts of the last user message and nothing else: no earlier turns, no system prompt, no tool definitions, no files.
- **Images aren’t sent..** A message that is only an image has no words to classify, so no intent matches. To route by images, use the rule’s has an image condition.
- **Agent reminders are removed..** `<system-reminder>…</system-reminder>` blocks, which Claude Code adds to your message, are stripped. Other text an agent puts in the same message is kept.
- **Long messages are shortened..** Over 4,000 characters, jianmu keeps the first 3,000 and the last 1,000, joined by `…`. The start and the end usually say what is being asked.
- **The request settings..** An OpenAI-style chat completion, not streamed, with `temperature 0`, `max_tokens 2048` and User-Agent `jianmu-router/1`. When jianmu knows the classifier’s reasoning levels, it asks for the least: `none` if the model has it, else its lowest level (for example `low`). When the levels aren’t known, nothing is sent and the vendor’s default applies. jianmu translates it for the classifier’s provider, like any other request, so an Anthropic, Gemini or other model works too.

## When it can’t say

A classifier is a helper, not a gate. Whatever happens to it, the turn is still answered: the intent rules just don’t match.

| What happens | What jianmu does |
| --- | --- |
| It answers `0` | No intent matches. Rules without an intent and the group’s usual order decide. |
| No answer within the configured timeout | Treated as a failure: no intent matches, and the turn goes on at once. |
| An error (quota, 5xx, bad key) | Its provider’s own failover is tried first, within the configured timeout. If it still fails, no intent matches. |
| An answer that isn’t a number from 0 to n | No intent matches this turn. The classifier did answer, so it isn’t rested: the next turn asks it again. |
| An error or a timeout | That classifier model is left alone for 30 s: turns in that time don’t wait on it, and the trace says it wasn’t asked. The first good answer clears this. |
| The message has no words | Not asked. No intent matches. |

Each case is written in the turn’s trace with the reason. An intent rule can therefore make a turn go to a different model than you hoped, but it can’t make it fail.

## The rest of the turn

A turn is often dozens of requests: the agent calls a tool, sends the result back, calls another, and so on. jianmu deals with them like this:

- **Held..** Every request within the turn goes to the model the turn began on, and the classifier isn’t asked again. Switching models mid-turn would throw away what the vendor cached of the conversation (prompt caching), and some vendors reject reasoning that another one wrote.
- **Failover sticks..** If the rule’s model failed and another member answered, that member keeps the rest of the turn (with Stays on *Auto*, *Session* or *Within a turn*). The rule decides again at your next message.
- **Outgrown..** The one exception: if the conversation grows within the turn to 95% of the current model’s context, jianmu checks the rules again, keeping the classifier’s earlier answer. If a rule sends it to a model with *more* context, it moves. It never moves to a model with less.
- **Waits..** If jianmu didn’t see the turn begin (it was started or restarted in the middle of one), or the rule that decided it was removed or now sends to another model, no rule moves the turn. The rules decide again at your next message.
- **Subagents..** A subagent’s turns are decided on their own, from the subagent’s own messages. A rule can send a subagent elsewhere while its agent stays where it is.

Decisions are kept in memory for 24 hours after a conversation’s last request. Restarting jianmu clears them, and the next message decides afresh.

## Reading the trace

The Routing tab shows each group’s latest request: who answered it, and under How the last request was routed, why.

The lines you can see about intent:

| The trace says | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| … was asked which of “A”, “B” turn 1 is, and said “B” (in 323 ms). | The classifier was asked, with these candidates, and named B. |
| … and said none (…). | It answered 0. |
| … (said before, for the same message). | The answer came from the 10-minute cache, so no call was made. |
| … was to tell which … but couldn’t — *reason* — so no rule with an intent matches it. | It failed. The reason is the error, the timeout, what it answered, or that it is resting after a failure. |
| Turn N begins and rule R matches — asks for “B” — so M goes first … | The rule that won, and the model put first. |
| Rule R matches, but M has no account or key that can take this request, so the group’s order stands. | No account or key for the rule’s model can take this request. |
| Rule R (…) sent turn N to M as it began; the turn stays there. | A tool round within the turn, held on its decision. |
| This turn began before jianmu saw it, so the rules wait for the next one. | See *Waits* above. |

The classifier’s own calls appear in Usage under the agent *jianmu*, with their tokens and cost, so you can see what classifying costs.

## Latency, cost, privacy

- **Latency..** Only the first request of a turn waits for the classifier, typically a few hundred milliseconds on a fast provider (323 ms in the screenshot) with a configured timeout of 8 seconds by default. Tool rounds within the turn, turns where no intent could decide, and cached answers add nothing.
- **Cost..** One short call per turn: roughly the size of your message plus the intents in, and one or two tokens out. In the example above that was 212 tokens in and 1 out. With a subscription model as the classifier, these calls count against that subscription’s limits.
- **Privacy..** The text of your message (up to about 4,000 characters) goes to the classifier’s provider. To keep it on your machine, use a local model from Ollama or LM Studio as the classifier. jianmu keeps only a hash of the message and the answer, in memory, for 10 minutes. The message itself isn’t stored or logged.

## Writing good intents

- **Describe the request, not the model..** Write “writing or fixing tests”, not “hard tasks for Opus”. The classifier sees only your words and the message.
- **Keep kinds apart..** If two intents overlap (“a question”, “a question about the code”), a small model will choose between them unpredictably. Merge them, or make the difference plain.
- **Few and broad beats many and narrow..** Two to five intents are easy for an 8B model. Up to 200 characters each is allowed, but a few words are usually enough.
- **Order still matters..** Only the first matching rule counts, so put a rule that must win (such as a long-context rule) above the intent rules. The classifier is then skipped whenever that rule holds.
- **“None” is a real answer..** A turn that fits no intent goes to the group’s usual order, so let that order be your default choice.
- **Any language..** Intents and messages can be in any language the classifier understands. The fixed prompt is in English, and small models read mixed languages well.
- **Choosing a classifier..** Pick a small, fast model without reasoning: Llama 3.1 8B on Groq, a Flash-Lite, nano or mini model, Claude Haiku, DeepSeek’s non-reasoning chat model, or a local model. A reasoning model is slower; jianmu asks it for its least reasoning and leaves it 2048 tokens, but a slow one can still miss the configured timeout. Check the trace for a few turns: if it guesses wrong, rewrite the intents before switching models.

## Numbers

| What | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Classifier timeout | 8 s by default; configurable from 1 to 60 s, including its provider’s failover |
| Rest after a failure | 30 s, per classifier model |
| Answer cache | 10 min, per classifier + intents + message; in memory |
| Turn decisions kept | 24 h after the conversation’s last request; in memory |
| Message sent | Up to 4,000 characters; longer is first 3,000 + last 1,000 |
| Classifier request | temperature 0, max_tokens 2048, the least reasoning the model has, not streamed |
| Intent length | Up to 200 characters; spaces collapsed, compared without case |
| Outgrown | At 95% of the current model’s context, only to a model with more |

## FAQ

### Is this embeddings or a vector search?

No. There is no embedding model, no similarity threshold, no keyword list and nothing to train. The classifier is an ordinary chat model that reads your intents and your message and answers with a number. It is only as good as that model and your wording, and the trace shows every answer.

### Does it look at the whole conversation?

No, only the message you just sent. So a follow-up like “now do the same for the other file” is judged on those words alone. Give that turn a clearer message, or add an intent that fits follow-ups.

### My agent made 40 requests for one message. Was the classifier asked 40 times?

No, once. The other 39 carried tool results, so they belong to the same turn and follow its decision. You can see this in the trace (“the turn stays there”) and in Usage (one *jianmu* call).

### Can a turn switch models halfway?

Only in two cases: the model it is on fails and another member takes over, or the conversation outgrows the model’s context and a rule sends it to one with more room. Intent is never re-asked mid-turn.

### What if the classifier is down or slow?

The turn still goes through. After waiting up to the configured timeout (8 s by default), no intent matches and the group’s other rules and order decide. For the next 30 s jianmu doesn’t ask that classifier again, so turns don’t each wait out the timeout. The trace gives the reason.

### Why did the turn not go to the rule’s model when the classifier named its intent?

Check the trace. The usual causes are:

- a rule above it matched first;
- another condition on the rule didn’t hold (tokens, images, reasoning or agent);
- no account or key for the rule’s model could take this request;
- it was a tool round in a turn that began elsewhere;
- jianmu didn’t see the turn begin (“the rules wait”).

### Two rules have the same intent. What happens?

The intent is offered to the classifier once. If it is chosen, the first of those rules whose other conditions hold wins. Use this to send, for example, “writing or fixing tests” from Codex to one model and from Claude Code to another.

### Does changing a rule affect a turn already running?

No. Saving applies from the next turn. A turn whose rule you removed, or pointed at another model, keeps where it is until then; the trace says the rules wait.

### Can the classifier be a routing group, or one of the group’s own models?

It can’t be a group: it must be one model, `provider/model`, which jianmu checks when you save. It can be any model jianmu has, including one of the group’s members, a subscription model or a local model.

### Can I use a reasoning model?

Yes, if it answers within the configured timeout (8 s by default). jianmu asks it for the least reasoning it has (`none`, else its lowest level) and leaves 2048 tokens, so thinking doesn’t crowd out the answer. A small, fast model is still the better choice: cheaper, and every turn waits for it.

### How well does it work with real models?

We ran 20 real coding messages (English and Chinese: quick questions, test work, and ordinary coding tasks, including “Fix the bug in parseTokens and add a test for it”) through a group with two intent rules. DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.3 Flash and MiMo v2.6 Flash each classified all 20 correctly; the median classifier time was 0.75 s, 1.3 s and 1.9 s. Gemini 3.8 Flash through one reseller took 11 s even at `low` reasoning, so with the default 8 s timeout every turn timed out and routed as if there were no intents — the trace said so each time. That is the pattern to expect: a wrong classifier costs you the routing, never the turn.

### Does retrying the same message ask again?

Not within 10 minutes: the same message with the same intents and the same classifier is answered from the cache, and the trace says “said before”. Changing an intent or the classifier makes it ask again.

### Which agents does it work with?

Any agent that sends to a routing group through jianmu: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and the rest. Turns are detected from the request itself (a message with text and no tool results), whatever API the agent speaks.

### Is my message stored anywhere?

jianmu keeps a hash of it (for the cache) and the classifier’s answer, in memory only. The text goes to the classifier’s provider, like any request, under that provider’s terms. The classifier’s usage record holds its token counts, not the text.

### How accurate is it?

That depends on the classifier and on how distinct your intents are. With a few clearly different kinds, a small model picks well; with overlapping ones it will sometimes guess. Since a wrong or missing answer only changes which model answers, start with two or three broad intents, watch the trace for a day and adjust the wording.

Questions or a setup worth sharing? Ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues). Routing groups in general are covered in [Get started](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/start#routing).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/masking

# Privacy masking

jianmu can mask what your agents send before it leaves this computer. API keys, passwords and tokens, and when you ask, emails, phone numbers and words of your own, go to the vendor as placeholders such as `{{API_KEY_es6eu6jk}}`. In the reply each placeholder turns back into its value, so your agent and your files keep the real thing and the vendor never sees it. It runs on this computer, in jianmu’s gateway, and is **off by default**.

> **It covers what goes through jianmu.** An agent [connected to jianmu](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/start) sends its requests through the gateway, and they are masked whichever provider or account answers. An agent that calls a vendor directly, not through jianmu, is not covered.

## Turn it on

1. **Open the page.** Go to Settings → Privacy.
2. **Mask secrets.** Under What to mask, set Mask secrets to On: API keys, private keys, tokens and passwords.
3. **Personal data, if you want it.** Set Mask personal data to On for emails, phone numbers, ID and bank card numbers. Each further kind of personal data then gets its own switch below it.
4. **Your own words.** In Masked words, list names, codenames or hosts to keep from vendors, one on each row (several pasted with commas between become a row each). Masked words in any case makes *Nightjar* mask *NIGHTJAR* too. A secret jianmu doesn’t know, such as your gateway’s own keys, goes under Masking rules: what it starts with, or a regular expression.
5. **Try it.** Paste a text into Try it to see exactly what the vendor would get. What you paste there isn’t kept.

It applies from the next request, with no restart and nothing to change in your agent. The work is done by the built-in plugin Privacy masking (`redact`, in Settings → Plugins), which is on whenever any masking is asked for.

There is no CLI command for it. Without the window (`jianmu serve`, [Docker](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/docker)), open the same page with `jianmu web`, or set it in `~/.config/jianmu/settings.json` (`/config/jianmu/settings.json` in Docker). The masker reads the file on every request:

```
{
  "redact": true,
  "redactPersonal": true,
  "redactWords": ["Nightjar", "db.acme-corp.cn"]
}
```

## What is masked

| Switch | What it finds |
| --- | --- |
| Mask secrets | Private key blocks (`-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----`). API keys by their shape: `sk-…` (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter), `ghp_`/`github_pat_`, `glpat-`, `AIza…`, `xox…-`, `sk_live_`, `AKIA`/`ASIA`, `hf_`, `gsk_`, `xai-`, `npm_`, `pypi-`, `dop_v1_`, `SG.`, and relay keys like `oc_sk_…`. JWTs. The password in `user:password@host`. The value of a field named for a secret, as `.env` files and configs have them: `DB_PASSWORD=…`, `api_key: …`, `client_secret`, `token`, `credential`. Your own Masking rules. Wallet private keys by the shape their wallets export: a Bitcoin WIF, a BIP32 `xprv`, an Ethereum or TRON `0x` key, a Solana key or `id.json` keypair, a Sui `suiprivkey1…`, an Aptos `ed25519-priv-0x…`, a Stellar seed, a NEAR `ed25519:…` key, a Nostr `nsec1…`, an age identity, a Zcash extended spending key, and a 12 to 25 word seed phrase after *seed* or *mnemonic* whose every word is in the BIP39 list. A key with no prefix of its own is masked only when it checks out: a WIF or `xprv` by its checksum, a Solana key by its public half, a Stellar seed by its CRC, so a Solana transaction signature goes as written. A `0x` key has the shape of a transaction hash, so it is masked only after a key&rsquo;s name (`PRIVATE_KEY=`, `--private-key`, `new Wallet(…)`, 私钥); a hash, a storage slot or a sha256 sum goes as written. An exchange&rsquo;s API key, secret and `passphrase` go by their fields&rsquo; names. |
| Mask personal data | Emails, mainland China mobile numbers (not an 11-digit id: one under `order_id` or after 订单号 goes as written), Chinese ID numbers and bank card numbers whose checksum adds up. Also on by default: US Social Security numbers, passport numbers (after *passport*, 护照 or パスポート), IBANs, birthdays (next to *birthday*, *DOB* or 生日, and over a year ago, so today&rsquo;s date stays), MAC addresses and serial numbers (after *S/N*). Off until you turn them on, since agents send them in nearly every request: the user name in home folders (sent as a made-up name, the same every turn, so the model reads a real folder rather than a placeholder), user and computer names (`user@host`), public IP addresses (sent as a name such as `public-ip-kvxqmrtz`, so the model still knows the address is public and connects with it, and the real address goes back into its commands) and cloud storage buckets. A wallet or contract address (`0x` and 40 hex digits) is public and goes as written; a private key is still masked. |
| Masked words | Each word you listed, exactly, as `{{TERM_…}}`. A date, such as *1990-05-12*, matches that day however it is written: *1990/5/12*, *1990.05.12*, *1990年5月12日*, *19900512*, *May 12, 1990*, and *13/05/1990* style only where the day can’t be read as a month. Never another date or a version like *1990.5.12.1*. |
| Find with a local model | Under How it’s found. A model on this computer finds what no rule can: a name or an address in free text. It is on unless you turned it off, and AstrLink Guard downloads with the first masked request; until it is on disk, the rules mask alone. It needs Mask secrets or Mask personal data on, and finds under the same switches. The menu beside it picks the model: AstrLink Guard (Chinese and English, a 39 MB download, few false alarms in code, on a Mac it runs on the Neural Engine; the default) or OpenAI’s Privacy Filter (1.6 GB, uses the GPU, masks more ordinary values in code). Confidence threshold under it is how sure the model must be before a value is masked: Privacy Filter’s default is 0.5, AstrLink Guard’s 0.8, its publisher’s. Higher masks fewer ordinary values, and lets more real names and addresses through: the rules after the model drop most false alarms already, so the default is where we measured the fewest real values lost. |

A placeholder is the kind plus eight characters of a keyed hash. The same value gets the same placeholder every time, so the conversation reads the same turn after turn and the vendor’s prompt cache stays valid. The values are held in memory only.

## An example

With Mask secrets and Mask personal data on and *Nightjar* in Masked words, your agent sends:

```
Deploy Nightjar with OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-8fK2mQx7Lp4Rt9Vw3Yz6Ab1Cd, then mail li.wei@acme-corp.cn or call 13800138000.
```

```
Deploy {{TERM_5hmsrhdc}} with OPENAI_API_KEY={{API_KEY_srhjgvja}}, then mail {{EMAIL_eh5um6mb}} or call {{PHONE_uf7iy2qq}}.
```

When the model answers *“I set OPENAI_API_KEY to {{API_KEY_srhjgvja}} in .env”*, your agent reads the real key there, in streamed text and tool-call arguments alike, so the file it writes has the real key. A placeholder the model rewrote a little (spaces inside the braces, another case) is still turned back.

## Check that it works

- **Before:.** Try it on Settings → Privacy shows the text as the vendor would get it, with each value’s kind.
- **Each request:.** a shield badge with a count appears on the request in the Gateway page’s recent calls and in the Routing log. Point at it for the kinds; click it to open the request’s record.
- **Over time:.** Insights → Masking (also What was masked on the Privacy page) shows the values masked over 7 or 30 days by kind, agent and provider, and each request’s text as the vendor saw it, placeholders marked.

The records are kept in `~/.config/jianmu/masking` for 30 days: the agent, provider, model, and each placeholder’s kind, length and first characters, never the value.

## When a value is found

Under When a value is found, choose per kind:

- Mask (the default): sent as a placeholder.
- Warn: sent as written, and the badge counts it in amber.
- Block: the request is held back with a 400, *“jianmu held this request back: Settings › Privacy blocks API_KEY, and it has one (sk-…, 33 characters). Nothing was sent.”* The message never has the value.

A value the task needs as it is, such as a team address or a test key, goes in Never mask: it is sent as written wherever it is found whole.

## What it leaves alone, and limits

- **Thinking stays as the vendor wrote it..** A thinking block with its signature, Gemini’s thoughts and Responses’ encrypted reasoning are sealed by the vendor and go back unchanged, so the signature still matches. Only values already masked elsewhere in the request are swapped in them.
- **Ids and tool definitions go as written:.** model ids, message and call ids, UUIDs, tool names, MCP server names, and tool schemas (their descriptions are masked), so a vendor or a tool can still check them.
- **Images and file data are sent as they are..** Text inside a screenshot is not masked.
- **It fails closed..** If masking is on and can’t run (the Privacy masking plugin turned off by hand, or the local model you turned on can’t answer), the request gets a 503 that says nothing was sent. It is never sent unmasked instead. The model on by default that can’t answer leaves the rules to mask alone.
- **A provider can skip it..** Send requests unmasked on a provider sends its requests as written: a model on this computer or your local network (Ollama, LM Studio), and, if you choose, any other provider, a subscription or a plugin’s provider too. Turned on for one that isn’t local, the editor says its vendor gets your requests unmasked. A request that can fall back to a provider still masked is masked. `jianmu provider set ollama unmasked=yes` does the same.
- **Or send what masking would change to one of them..** In Settings › Privacy, Instead of masking, send to picks such a model. An agent’s request that masking would change then goes to it as written, so it can answer about the real names, and a request with nothing to mask goes where it was going. If that model fails, the request fails: it is never masked and sent to a vendor instead. Off by default.
- **The model sees placeholders..** It can’t read or reason about a masked value; it can only pass it on. Put a value it must read under Never mask.
- **Rules find shapes..** A phone number in another country’s format or a name in free text needs Find with a local model, or your own Masked words and Masking rules. Try your own text in Try it first.

See also [Privacy](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/privacy) for everything jianmu sends by itself. The code is [internal/redact](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/tree/main/internal/redact) and [internal/masking](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/internal/masking/masking.go).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-desktop

# Claude Desktop on any model

Claude Desktop has a third-party gateway mode: no Anthropic sign-in, and its Code and Cowork tabs work on any plan. jianmu sets Desktop up in that mode with jianmu’s gateway, so Desktop runs on any model you have in jianmu: DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, an OpenAI key, or a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription.

In its gateway mode Claude Desktop sends every request to one address instead of Anthropic. jianmu writes that mode and a profile named jianmu, pointing at its gateway, `http://127.0.0.1:3425`, into Desktop’s configuration folders. The gateway speaks Anthropic’s Messages API and translates each request for the model you picked, streaming, tool calls and reasoning included. It works on macOS, Windows (the Store package too) and Linux.

## Turn it on

1. **Add providers in jianmu.** In the Providers tab, add an API key or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Choose jianmu on Claude Desktop’s row.** In the Agents tab, Claude Desktop’s row offers jianmu: Desktop’s third-party gateway, Code and Cowork on jianmu’s models, no Anthropic sign-in.
3. **Quit and reopen Claude Desktop.** Desktop reads this only as it starts.

```
jianmu claude-desktop jianmu      # Desktop on jianmu's gateway
jianmu claude-desktop default     # back to the Anthropic sign-in
```

## Pick a model

Desktop lists the gateway’s models when it starts, so its model picker shows the models you have in jianmu. A model with a 1M context window is listed once, as its 1M entry. After you add a provider in jianmu, quit and reopen Desktop to see its models.

## The Code tab’s tiers

The Code tab runs Claude Code, which asks for models by tier: opus, sonnet, haiku. Left unset, a tier runs on the chat’s model. Pick a model for a tier on Claude Desktop’s row, or from a terminal, and restart Desktop after a change:

```
jianmu claude-desktop sonnet deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
jianmu claude-desktop haiku deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash
```

A picked model runs with the prompt of the Claude model of its tier. The row also has a subagent model, which takes effect without a restart.

## Your chats and projects

Desktop keeps its gateway mode in a profile of its own, so chats and projects from your Anthropic sign-in don’t show while it runs on jianmu. Nothing is deleted, and switching back brings them back. To go on with them on jianmu, use Settings → Import in Desktop, which copies in your Claude.ai chats and projects and leaves the originals as they are.

## A separate Claude Jianmu app (Mac)

On a Mac, jianmu can run Desktop’s gateway mode in a folder of its own, started by `~/Applications/Claude Jianmu.app`. Your own Claude Desktop stays signed in with Anthropic, and both run side by side. It is off by default.

```
jianmu claude-desktop launcher add      # make Claude Jianmu.app
jianmu claude-desktop launcher remove
```

## Switch back

Take Claude Desktop’s row off jianmu, or run `jianmu claude-desktop default`, then quit and reopen Desktop. jianmu puts Desktop’s files back as they were, and your chats from before are there again.

## FAQ

### Do I need a Claude subscription for Cowork and the Code tab?

No. In gateway mode, Desktop’s Code and Cowork tabs work without an Anthropic sign-in, on whatever model jianmu serves.

### Can I use my ChatGPT subscription in Claude Desktop?

Yes. Sign in to ChatGPT in jianmu, and its GPT models appear in Desktop’s model picker after a restart.

### Why doesn’t Claude Desktop show a new model?

Desktop reads the model list as it starts. Quit and reopen it.

### Why is Claude Desktop in English on jianmu?

Desktop’s gateway-mode window has no translation of its own. Switching back brings your language back.

### Are my old chats gone?

No. They stay in Desktop’s own profile and come back when you switch back, or you can import them with Settings → Import.

The same models in the terminal: [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models) and [ChatGPT in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-chatgpt). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/openclaw

# OpenClaw on any model

OpenClaw answers you on WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord and more, on whatever model its config names. jianmu adds itself to OpenClaw as one provider, so OpenClaw can run on any model you have in jianmu: DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, an OpenAI key, or a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription, with no key pasted into OpenClaw.

OpenClaw keeps its settings in `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`. jianmu adds a provider named jianmu there: its gateway’s `/v1` address, OpenAI’s chat completions API, a key of OpenClaw’s own, and one entry per model you have in jianmu. Then it makes the model you pick OpenClaw’s default. The gateway translates each request for that model’s provider, tool calls and reasoning included.

## Connect OpenClaw

1. **Add providers in jianmu.** In the Providers tab, add an API key or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Pick a model on OpenClaw’s row.** In the Agents tab, choose a model on OpenClaw’s row. OpenClaw takes it up without a restart.

```
jianmu openclaw deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro    # OpenClaw on DeepSeek
jianmu openclaw                             # what OpenClaw runs on now
```

## Pick a model

In OpenClaw a model is named `provider/model`, so jianmu’s models show up as `jianmu/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro`, `jianmu/openai/gpt-6.1` and so on. jianmu sets the primary model and keeps your fallbacks. If your config has a list of allowed models, jianmu adds `jianmu/*` to it so its models aren’t refused. A model whose context jianmu doesn’t know is given 128K.

## Chats that already have a model

A change to the default model reaches new chats at once. A chat that already has a model keeps it: send `/model default` in that chat to move it onto the new one.

## What jianmu writes

Only `models.providers.jianmu`, the default model, and the allow list when you have one. Your other providers, channels and keys stay as you wrote them, and so do keys you add to jianmu’s provider yourself (headers, timeoutSeconds, a model’s maxTokens). A model set for one agent (`agents.entries.*.model`) stays yours, and a config split with `$include` isn’t changed.

jianmu finds the file where OpenClaw does: `$OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, else `openclaw.json` in `$OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, else `~/.openclaw-<profile>` for `$OPENCLAW_PROFILE`, else `~/.openclaw`. A file written in JSON5 that isn’t plain JSON is left alone, and jianmu says so.

## Switch back

Take OpenClaw’s row off jianmu, or run `jianmu openclaw default`. jianmu removes its provider and puts back the model OpenClaw ran on before, as long as jianmu’s model is still the default; a model you picked since stays.

## FAQ

### Can OpenClaw use my ChatGPT subscription?

Yes. Sign in to ChatGPT in jianmu and pick a GPT model on OpenClaw’s row. OpenClaw sends its requests to jianmu, which uses the subscription.

### Do I need to restart OpenClaw?

No. OpenClaw’s gateway takes up a change of models and default model by itself. Chats that already have a model keep it until you send /model default there.

### Does jianmu touch my channels or other providers?

No. It writes only its own provider, the default model and, if you have one, the allow list.

### I use an OpenClaw profile. Does jianmu find it?

Yes. It reads OPENCLAW_PROFILE, OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR, OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH and OPENCLAW_HOME the way OpenClaw does.

More agents on the same models: [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models), [Hermes Agent on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/hermes), [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models) and [nanobot on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/nanobot). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/hermes

# Hermes Agent on any model

Hermes Agent, from Nous Research, runs on the model its config.yaml names. jianmu adds itself to Hermes as one provider, so Hermes and each of its bots can run on any model you have in jianmu: DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, an OpenAI key, or a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription, with no key pasted into Hermes.

Hermes keeps its settings in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes` on Windows, or `$HERMES_HOME`). jianmu adds a provider named jianmu to its `providers`: the gateway, spoken to as chat completions, with your models in jianmu as its models. Then it points `model.provider` at it and sets `model.default` to the model you pick. The provider and model you had are kept aside and put back when you switch back.

## Connect Hermes

1. **Add providers in jianmu.** In the Providers tab, add an API key or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Pick a model on Hermes Agent’s row.** In the Agents tab, choose a model on Hermes Agent’s row.
3. **Restart open Hermes sessions.** Hermes reads its settings as it starts.

```
jianmu hermes deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro    # Hermes on DeepSeek
jianmu hermes                             # what Hermes runs on now
```

## Model and reasoning effort

In Hermes’s own model picker, jianmu’s models are named `jianmu/<provider>/<model>`. The row also sets the reasoning effort, the same setting as Hermes’s `/reasoning`: none, minimal, low, medium, high or xhigh. Left unset, Hermes asks for medium.

```
jianmu hermes effort high
jianmu hermes effort default    # back to Hermes's own
```

## Bots and profiles

Each Hermes bot is a profile with a config.yaml of its own. jianmu connects the profile `hermes` starts in: the one `$HERMES_HOME` names, else the one `hermes profile use` made sticky, else the default. It also adds its provider to every other profile, so jianmu’s models are in every bot’s picker. A bot’s own model is left as you set it. With more than one profile, each other bot gets a model picker of its own on the Agents page; a bot still on the model jianmu last set follows the next one, until you pick one for it.

## Your own models stay

Pick one of your own models in Hermes, or on the Agents page, and Hermes runs on it, but jianmu’s provider stays: Hermes is still connected, and its picker still offers jianmu’s models beside yours. Only switching back takes the provider out.

Hermes inside WSL on Windows is found too: jianmu writes the distro’s `~/.hermes`, with the gateway at the address the distro reaches it.

## Switch back

Take Hermes Agent’s row off jianmu, or run `jianmu hermes default`. jianmu removes its provider from every profile, puts back the provider and model you had, and leaves each bot on a model it can start with. Connecting again puts the bots back on the models they had.

## FAQ

### Can Hermes Agent use my ChatGPT subscription?

Yes. Sign in to ChatGPT in jianmu and pick a GPT model on Hermes Agent’s row. Hermes sends its requests to jianmu, which uses the subscription.

### I picked a model in jianmu but my bot still uses the old one.

Restart the bot’s Hermes session: Hermes reads config.yaml as it starts. A bot you gave a model of its own on the Agents page doesn’t follow the main one.

### Why does Hermes still say connected after I picked my own model?

jianmu’s provider stays so its models remain in Hermes’s picker. Switch back to take it out.

### Does jianmu touch my other Hermes providers?

No. It adds its own provider and changes only model.provider, model.default and, when you set it, the reasoning effort.

More agents on the same models: [OpenClaw on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/openclaw), [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models) and [Cline on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/cline). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/cline

# Cline on any model

Cline runs on the provider and model in its settings. jianmu sets Cline’s built-in OpenAI-compatible provider to jianmu’s gateway, so Cline’s CLI, VS Code extension and desktop app can run on any model you have in jianmu: DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, an OpenAI key, or a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription, with no key pasted into Cline.

Cline keeps its providers in `~/.cline/data/settings/providers.json` (or under `$CLINE_DIR`). jianmu sets Cline’s own openai-compatible provider to the gateway’s address with a key of Cline’s own, makes it the provider in use, and lists jianmu’s models for it in `models.json`, in place of the one model that provider lists by itself. What was there, and the provider you used, are kept aside and put back when you switch back. The gateway translates each request for the model’s provider, tool calls and reasoning included.

## Connect Cline

1. **Add providers in jianmu.** In the Providers tab, add an API key or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Pick a model on Cline’s row.** In the Agents tab, choose a model on Cline’s row.
3. **Start a new Cline session.** Cline reads its provider as a session starts: open sessions keep the model they have, new ones use this.

```
jianmu cline deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro    # Cline on DeepSeek
jianmu cline                             # what Cline runs on now
```

## Model and reasoning effort

The row also sets the reasoning effort Cline asks for: none, low, medium, high or xhigh. None turns thinking off, as Cline’s own picker does.

```
jianmu cline effort high
jianmu cline effort default    # back to Cline's own
```

## The VS Code extension

Cline’s VS Code extension uses the same folder but reads the provider, model, address and key from its own state first: the Act and Plan modes’ provider and model, and the OpenAI-compatible key. jianmu sets those too, keeping what they were. The extension reads them once, as it starts, so after a change run Developer: Reload Window in VS Code.

## The desktop app

Cline’s desktop app keeps the model and effort you pick in its own composer and doesn’t read them from these files. jianmu’s models are in its picker, under jianmu: pick one there. jianmu’s row sets the CLI and the VS Code extension.

## Switch back

Take Cline’s row off jianmu, or run `jianmu cline default`. jianmu puts back the provider you used, the model list, and the extension’s settings as they were.

## FAQ

### Can Cline use my ChatGPT subscription?

Yes. Sign in to ChatGPT in jianmu and pick a GPT model on Cline’s row. Cline sends its requests to jianmu, which uses the subscription.

### I changed the model but Cline still uses the old one.

A session keeps the model it started with. Start a new one; for the VS Code extension, reload the window.

### Why doesn’t jianmu add its own provider to Cline?

Cline refuses a provider it doesn’t know when a session starts, so jianmu uses Cline’s built-in OpenAI-compatible provider instead.

### Does this work in Cline’s desktop app?

Its picker lists jianmu’s models under jianmu; pick the model there, since the app doesn’t read it from Cline’s files.

More agents on the same models: [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models), [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models), [Hermes Agent on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/hermes), [Goose on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/goose) and [Zoo Code on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/zoo-code). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/goose

# Goose on any model

Goose, Block’s open-source agent, runs on the provider and model in its config. jianmu adds itself to Goose as a custom provider, so Goose’s CLI and desktop app can run on any model you have in jianmu: DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, an OpenAI key, or a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription, with no key pasted into Goose.

Goose keeps its settings in `~/.config/goose/config.yaml` (under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` if set; `%APPDATA%\Block\goose\config` on Windows). jianmu writes a custom provider, `custom_providers/jianmu.json` beside it, with the gateway’s address, a key of Goose’s own and jianmu’s models, then makes it the provider Goose uses. The gateway translates each request for the model’s provider, tool calls and reasoning included. A Goose in WSL is set up the same way, reaching the gateway as the distro sees it.

## Connect Goose

1. **Add providers in jianmu.** In the Providers tab, add an API key or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Pick a model on Goose’s row.** In the Agents tab, choose a model on Goose’s row. The picker also lists the models of providers Goose is set up with itself.
3. **Restart Goose.** Goose loads its custom providers as it starts: quit and reopen the desktop app, and open `goose` sessions again.

```
jianmu goose deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro    # Goose on DeepSeek
jianmu goose                             # what Goose runs on now
```

## Model and thinking effort

Each model jianmu lists for Goose carries its context window, so Goose doesn’t have to guess it, and whether it takes a thinking level. The row also sets `GOOSE_THINKING_EFFORT`, the effort Goose asks of a model that thinks: off, low, medium, high or max.

```
jianmu goose effort high
jianmu goose effort default    # back to Goose's own
```

## What jianmu writes

Goose has two layouts for the provider in use: `active_provider` with `providers.jianmu.model`, and the older `GOOSE_PROVIDER` and `GOOSE_MODEL`. jianmu writes the one your config already uses. Keys you added to jianmu’s provider file yourself, such as `timeout_seconds`, `headers` or `toolshim`, stay when jianmu rewrites the models.

## Switch back

Pick one of your own providers’ models on Goose’s row, take the row off jianmu, or run `jianmu goose default`. Once Goose no longer uses a model of jianmu’s, jianmu removes its provider file.

## FAQ

### Can Goose use my ChatGPT subscription?

Yes. Sign in to ChatGPT in jianmu and pick a GPT model on Goose’s row. Goose sends its requests to jianmu, which uses the subscription.

### Goose doesn’t show jianmu’s models.

Goose reads custom providers only as it starts. Quit and reopen Goose, and start a new goose session.

### Does this work in the Goose desktop app?

Yes. The CLI and the desktop app read the same config, so both use the model on Goose’s row after a restart.

### Does it work with goose in WSL?

Yes. jianmu sets up a Goose in a WSL distro too, with the gateway’s address as the distro reaches it.

More agents on the same models: [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models), [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models), [Cline on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/cline) and [Droid on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/droid). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/droid

# Droid on any model

Droid, Factory’s coding agent, can run on custom models of your own. jianmu adds the models you have in jianmu to Droid as custom models, so droid can run on DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, an OpenAI key, or a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription, with no key pasted into Droid.

Droid keeps its settings in `~/.factory/settings.json` (under `$FACTORY_HOME_OVERRIDE` when set). jianmu adds one entry to its `customModels` per model in jianmu, with the gateway’s address and a key of Droid’s own, and sets `sessionDefaultSettings.model`, the model sessions start on. Each model goes on the API its provider speaks, Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Responses or Chat Completions, so the gateway relays it as it is. A droid in WSL is set up the same way, reaching the gateway as the distro sees it.

## Connect Droid

1. **Add providers in jianmu.** In the Providers tab, add an API key or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Pick a model on Droid’s row.** In the Agents tab, choose a model on Droid’s row.
3. **Restart droid.** Droid reads its settings as it starts: open sessions keep what they have, so start droid again.

```
jianmu droid deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro    # Droid on DeepSeek
jianmu droid                             # what Droid runs on now
```

## Models and thinking levels

jianmu’s models are in droid’s `/model` picker too, under Custom models, so you can switch inside a session. A model that reasons is given a starting effort, so the picker offers its levels (off, low, medium and high); one that is a model Droid has built in takes Droid’s own levels and default. A model whose name Droid reads as OpenAI’s or Claude’s is written on the API Droid expects for it, so Droid doesn’t warn at each session start.

## Your own models

Custom models you added yourself stay as they were, ahead of jianmu’s, so their ids don’t move. If you change a field of one of jianmu’s entries in settings.json, such as its name or effort, jianmu keeps your value; only the address and key are put back at each sync. The older `~/.factory/config.json` is left alone.

## Switch back

Take Droid’s row off jianmu, or run `jianmu droid default`. jianmu removes its custom models and puts back the default model you had.

## FAQ

### Can Droid use my ChatGPT subscription?

Yes. Sign in to ChatGPT in jianmu and pick a GPT model on Droid’s row. droid sends its requests to jianmu, which uses the subscription.

### I changed the model but droid still uses the old one.

Droid reads its settings as it starts. Restart droid, or switch with /model inside the session.

### Why does /model show no thinking levels for a model?

That model doesn’t reason. For one that does, jianmu gives it a starting effort, and droid then offers its levels.

### Will jianmu touch my own BYOK models?

No. Your custom models stay as they were and in front of jianmu’s.

More agents on the same models: [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models), [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models), [Goose on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/goose) and [Zed on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/zed). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/zed

# Zed on any model

Zed’s agent panel runs on the language model provider in its settings. jianmu adds itself to Zed as an OpenAI-compatible provider, so Zed’s agent can run on any model you have in jianmu: DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, an OpenAI key, or a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription, with no key pasted into Zed.

Zed keeps its settings in `~/.config/zed/settings.json` on macOS and Linux (under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` if set) and in `%APPDATA%\Zed` on Windows. jianmu adds `language_models.openai_compatible.jianmu`, with the gateway’s address and jianmu’s models, and sets `agent.default_model` to the model you pick. Zed reads the change as it runs. The gateway translates each request for the model’s provider, tool calls and reasoning included.

## Connect Zed

1. **Add providers in jianmu.** In the Providers tab, add an API key or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Pick a model on Zed’s row.** In the Agents tab, choose a model on Zed’s row.
3. **Open Zed’s agent panel.** The model is the panel’s default, and jianmu’s models are in its model picker under jianmu.

```
jianmu zed deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro    # Zed's agent on DeepSeek
jianmu zed                             # what Zed runs on now
```

## The API key

Zed keeps an OpenAI-compatible provider’s key in the system’s credential store, keyed by the provider’s address, not in settings.json. jianmu saves a key of Zed’s own there for you: in the Keychain on macOS, in the Secret Service on Linux and in the Credential Manager on Windows. If Zed still asks for an API key, restart Zed.

## Models and thinking

Each model carries its context window and reply limit, so Zed knows when to compact, and whether it takes images. A model that thinks is written with `reasoning_effort` high, or the strongest level it has, so Zed shows its thinking switch and levels. A level you set on a model in settings.json yourself, `none` included, stays when jianmu rewrites the list. If Zed reaches the gateway through a proxy of yours, jianmu keeps that address.

## Switch back

Pick one of Zed’s own models on its row, take the row off jianmu, or run `jianmu zed default`. jianmu puts back the default model, and the provider entry, you had before.

## FAQ

### Can Zed use my ChatGPT subscription?

Yes. Sign in to ChatGPT in jianmu and pick a GPT model on Zed’s row. Zed sends its requests to jianmu, which uses the subscription.

### Zed asks for an API key for jianmu.

jianmu saved the key in the system credential store. Restart Zed so it reads it.

### Why doesn’t Zed show a thinking switch for a model?

That model doesn’t think. For one that does, jianmu sets reasoning_effort, and Zed then shows the switch.

### Does this change Zed’s edit predictions?

No. jianmu sets the agent panel’s default model and adds a provider; edit predictions are left as they were.

More agents on the same models: [Models in OpenCode](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/opencode-models), [Models in Claude Code](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/claude-code-models), [Droid on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/droid) and [Crush on any model](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/crush). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).
