- **Sign-in..** A server that needs OAuth is signed in to once, in jianmu. Agents then reach it through jianmu’s gateway at `/mcp/<name>`.
- **This computer only..** Turn off Sync to your other computers for a server that should stay here (`jianmu library mcp local <name> on`).

With the [MCP router](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/mcp-router) on, each agent gets one server named `jianmu` in place of these entries, and jianmu runs each command server once for all of them. It is off by default.

## Skills

A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` in it. The agent reads each skill’s name and description and loads the rest when a task needs it. Add one from GitHub, any git repository, a folder on this computer, or the market on the Skills tab.

| Agent | Folder |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/skills` |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/skills` |
| OpenCode | `skills` in its config folder |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/skills` |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/skills` |
| Goose | `~/.agents/skills` |

### Links or copies

Give skills as sets how a skill reaches an agent, for every agent or, under By agent, for one:

- **Links.** (the default). The agent’s folder links to the library’s copy, so an update reaches every agent at once. On Windows without the right to make links, a junction is used.
- **Copies..** Each agent gets a folder of its own, for tools that don’t follow links. A copy is made again when the library’s skill changes. If the agent, or you, edit a copy, the next sync takes the newest edit into the library and gives it to the other agents. An edit that loses to a newer one is kept with the backups.

A skill folder of your own with the same name is never written over: the page asks whether to use the library’s or keep yours.

### Editing and updates

- **Edit.** opens a skill’s files on the page; Save (or ⌘S) writes them. The command line has no editor.
- **Updates..** When you open the Skills tab, skills from GitHub are checked for updates if 12 hours have passed since the last check (`jianmu library skill update` checks now). A skill you changed is never replaced without asking.
- **Put skills in..** Skills go to each ticked agent’s own folder (the default), or also into `~/.agents/skills`, which Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Crush, Droid, Kimi Code and other tools read.
- **Off here..** A skill can be turned off on this computer only; a sync from another computer doesn’t turn it back on.

## Subagents

A subagent is a helper the main agent can hand a task to. It has a name, a description and a prompt. jianmu writes it as a file in each ticked agent’s subagent folder. The main agent reads every subagent’s **description** and decides itself when to call one, so the description should say plainly what it is for and when to use it.

- **Name:.** 2 to 50 lowercase letters, digits and `-`. A few names are reserved, such as `default` and `main`.
- **Description:.** required, up to 1,000 characters.
- **Prompt:.** required. It becomes the subagent’s instructions.
- **Model:.** optional. See Subagent models.

| Agent | File | Skills, MCP servers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/agents/<name>.md` | the ones you pick |
| Codex | `~/.codex/agents/<name>.toml` | all the agent has |
| OpenCode | `agents/<name>.md` in its config folder | all the agent has |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/agents/<name>.md` | all the agent has |
| Qwen Code | `agents/<name>.md` in its folder | all the agent has |
| Droid | `~/.factory/droids/<name>.md` | MCP servers you pick; all skills |
| Grok | `agents/<name>.md` in its folder | all the agent has |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/agents/<name>.md` | all the agent has |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/agents/<name>.agent.md` | all the agent has |

- Only Claude Code limits a subagent to the skills you pick, and only Claude Code and Droid to the MCP servers you pick. Elsewhere a subagent has everything its agent has.
- Cursor: only the Cursor app reads `~/.cursor/agents`. `cursor-agent` reads only a project’s `.cursor/agents`.
- Kimi Code, Goose, Crush, Qoder, CodeBuddy, iFlow and Kiro have no user-wide subagent folder, so they get none. Agents in WSL get none either.
- If you edit a file jianmu wrote, it becomes yours and jianmu stops changing it. A file of your own with the same name is never written over; the page shows a problem instead.

## Subagent models

A subagent’s Model field is written only for **Codex**. Every other agent runs its subagents on the model it picks itself, and the page says so. Left empty, the field reads Picked by the agent.

For Codex, the model goes into the subagent’s `.toml` file. Codex lays that file over the spawn, so requests carry that model and jianmu’s gateway routes them like any other request. You can pick any model in Codex’s list, a jianmu `provider/model`, or a routing group (`group/<id>`).

### Codex’s subagent model on the Agents page

Codex’s row on the Agents page has a subagent model of its own, for every subagent Codex starts:

- **Lead’s pick.** (the default). The main agent picks each subagent’s model, one of Codex’s own too. A subagent it names no model for runs on the main agent’s model. A resumed subagent stays on the model it started on.
- **Same as the lead..** Every subagent runs on the main agent’s model.
- **A model or a group..** Every subagent runs on it, even when the main agent names another.

> **The Agents page wins.** When that setting is anything but Lead’s pick, the gateway sends every Codex subagent request to it, over a Library subagent’s own model too. The Library editor then says so. Picking a model there also removes `default_subagent_model` from Codex’s config.

Codex’s own `[agents] default_subagent_model` in `config.toml` is a different thing: only the model a subagent starts on when the main agent names none. One exception to all of the above: a task the ChatGPT backend has sealed stays on the model it asked for, unless the setting is a ChatGPT account’s model.

Claude Code has its own order: the model the main agent names in its call, then the subagent file’s `model:`, then `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` (which Claude Code’s row on the Agents page can set), then the session’s model.

## Hooks

A hook is a command an agent runs at a point in its turn: a notification when it finishes, a formatter after it edits a file. Pick a portable event (turn end, after a tool, before a tool, on a prompt, at session start) and jianmu writes it under each agent’s own name for that event. Only Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Grok Build and Grok App take hooks. A hook entry you change becomes yours.

## RTK

The RTK tab turns on [RTK](https://www.rtk-ai.app/) per agent: the agent’s shell commands run through RTK, which shortens their output to save tokens. jianmu can install RTK for you; turning it off works with RTK gone.

## billion-context

The billion-context tab turns on [billion-context](https://github.com/ranxianglei/billion-context)’s plugin per agent: it folds older turns of a long session into summaries the model can open again, so the session stays inside the model’s window. It is offered for Pi, omp, OpenCode, Claude Code, Hermes, DeepSeek Harness and Zed, whose requests still go through jianmu with it on. jianmu can install it for you (`npm install -g billion-context --prefix=~/.local`) and runs its own installer and remover; turning it off puts back what the install changed in the agent’s settings. An agent turned on here can’t also run billion-context-pi or opencode-acp.

For Claude Code, billion-context’s install turns Claude Code’s own auto-compaction off. jianmu turns it back on, so a session billion-context doesn’t fold, such as one in the Claude desktop app’s Code tab, compacts instead of stopping at “Prompt is too long”. A `DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT` you set yourself is left as it is.

Zed has no billion-context plugin, and Hermes’ and DeepSeek Harness’ plugins only catch HTTPS traffic, which jianmu’s local address isn’t. Turned on, jianmu runs `bili start` and points the agent’s jianmu provider at `http://127.0.0.1:8787/bili/` followed by jianmu’s address, the route billion-context documents for any client; for Hermes and DeepSeek Harness, in every profile that has jianmu’s provider. Pick one of jianmu’s models for the agent on the Agents page first, and restart it after turning it on or off.

The card shows how many tokens billion-context saved, in its own count: the net savings its dashboard shows, after the rebuilds a fold causes and the summaries’ cost, with how many folds and sessions, over every session it ran on this computer. jianmu asks a running billion-context for it (`/__bili/overview`); when none runs, the card shows the last count it read and when. It shows nothing until billion-context has run for an agent.

## What jianmu touches

- Only what it wrote: the text between its markers, entries it recorded, files it marked as its own.
- Never a file, entry or skill of yours with the same name. The page shows the clash and lets you choose.
- Anything it replaces goes to the backups first.

Projects can get skills and MCP servers too, in the project’s own folders (such as `.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills`, `.mcp.json` or `.codex/config.toml`). From a terminal, `jianmu library project add .` adds the folder you are in, `jianmu library project skill add . pdf docx` gives it skills, `jianmu library project skill rm . pdf` takes one away, and `jianmu library project skills .` lists them.

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/mcp-router

# MCP router

The MCP servers you add in jianmu’s Library are normally written into each agent’s own config, one entry per server. With the **MCP router** on, each agent is given a single server named `jianmu` instead, and jianmu passes each call on to the Library server behind it. It is **off by default**.

- **Set up once..** A server written once in the Library reaches every agent and app through one entry.
- **Run once..** A command server (one started as a program, such as `npx …`) runs once in jianmu, not once in each agent. A server with no calls for 10 minutes is stopped and starts again on the next call.
- **One address for other apps..** Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf or an app on another computer can connect to jianmu and use every Library server.

Tools appear in the agent as `server__tool`. Only tools are served (no resources or prompts), and a tool you turned off in the Library is neither listed nor run.

## Turn it on

1. **Open the page.** Go to Library → MCP.
2. **Switch it on.** Below the server list, turn on MCP router. Each agent that has Library servers ticked and can reach a server over HTTP (Streamable HTTP) gets one `jianmu` entry at `/mcp/jianmu/hub/<agent>` on jianmu’s gateway, and those servers’ own entries are taken out of its config.
3. **Restart your agents.** An agent reads the change when it starts again.

Turning it off writes each server’s own entry back, removes only the `jianmu` entry jianmu wrote, and stops every server the router started. From the command line:

```
jianmu library mcp router on
jianmu library mcp router off
```

`jianmu library` lists which agents are given the router and which keep their own entries, with why.

## Other apps

With the router on, the Other apps row shows an address ending in `/mcp/jianmu/hub`, which serves every server in the Library. Connect… opens a sheet with a ready entry to copy for Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf or any app that takes a JSON MCP config; in the app window, Cursor and VS Code also have Add, which opens the app to confirm. An app on another computer needs a gateway key, as every request from your network does (see [Remote jianmu](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/remote)).

> **Command servers run on this computer.** Anyone holding a gateway key on your network can call them through the router, with your rights here. Only share keys with people you trust.

## Agents that keep their own entries

These agents keep each server’s own entry, and the Library page says which and why:

- **No remote servers..** The agent can’t reach an MCP server over HTTP, such as Claude Desktop.
- **A server named jianmu..** One of your Library servers is itself called `jianmu`, so the names would clash.
- **Its own jianmu entry..** The agent already has an entry called `jianmu` that jianmu didn’t write; it is left as it is.

## When to use it

- **Turn it on.** when you use several agents with the same servers, when command servers start many copies of themselves, or when you want editors and other computers to use your Library.
- **Leave it off.** if you use one agent, if you want each agent to talk to its servers directly, or if you’d rather nothing else on your network can reach your command servers. Every call goes through jianmu, so jianmu needs to be running.

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/remote

# Remote jianmu

One jianmu can serve several computers. Sign in and set up providers and routing groups once, on the computer that keeps them (your desktop, a server, a [NAS in Docker](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/docker)), and on every other computer add that jianmu as a provider of its own: a **Remote jianmu**.

|  | The shared jianmu | Each other computer’s jianmu |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Providers, subscriptions, keys | kept and signed in here | uses them through the Remote jianmu |
| Routing groups | made here | picked as `office/group/…` |
| Agents | its own | still wired by this computer’s jianmu |
| Usage and quotas | counted and read here | shown here, named with the remote |

The computer you sit at still runs jianmu: it wires that computer’s agents, picks their models and keeps their sessions. Only the models come from the other one.

## 1. Share the main jianmu

1. **Turn on sharing.** On the computer that keeps your providers: Settings → Network and sharing → Share on local network → On. jianmu then listens on the local network and makes a gateway key named Jianmu. The Address row below the switch shows where other computers reach it, such as `http://192.168.1.20:3425`.
2. **Make a key for each computer.** Gateway → Gateway keys, or `jianmu gateway-key add "Laptop"`, which prints its `sk-jianmu-key-…`. Each key can have its own daily, weekly or monthly limit and its own models, and its calls are counted under its name.

While sharing is off, a desktop jianmu listens on its own computer only, and other computers can’t reach it. A jianmu in Docker is reached through its published port instead, and asks every caller outside its container for a gateway key, shared or not; see [Docker](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/docker#share).

## 2. Add it on the other computer

You need the address and a key from step 1. Any of these does it:

- **The app:.** on the Providers tab press ＋ Add provider, pick Remote jianmu under Another computer’s jianmu (the last heading), then give its address and the key.
- **The TUI.** (`jianmu tui`): on the Providers page press `a`, pick Remote jianmu, then type its address and key. On its row, `w` changes the address and `m` fetches its list again.
- **The CLI:.**

```
jianmu provider add remote-jianmu sk-jianmu-key-… url=http://192.168.1.20:3425 id=office
jianmu models            # office/… are the shared jianmu's
jianmu provider refresh office   # fetch its list again
```

`id=` names the provider here, and so begins its models’ ids (`office/…`). The address can be typed as `192.168.1.20:3425` (plain `http://` is assumed), with `/v1` after it, or as the root: jianmu puts every API on it either way. Add one Remote jianmu for each computer you share from, with a different id.

## What you get

- **Its models.** , as its own agents are shown them: `office/relay-a/claude-sonnet-5`, labelled `Claude Sonnet 5 · Relay A · office`. The ids stay ids; only the labels carry the names. Pick them for an agent here like any other model.
- **Its routing groups.** , as `office/group/…`. The group decides on the shared jianmu, with its accounts.
- **Every API..** A request goes on in the API the agent spoke (Anthropic Messages and token counting, Responses, Chat Completions). A model that the shared jianmu’s provider serves on another API only is turned into that API once, never on both computers. Responses go over HTTP, SSE included, not WebSocket.
- **Images and video..** Its image and video models are found by themselves and served through its image generation and edit, and video, APIs.
- **System One..** Its decision models (Jev, Clef, and models with names of your own) are set up at its `/v1/systemone` and appear as decision models, not chat models. Refresh the provider’s list to find new ones. A bare `office` asks the first decision model listed.
- **Embeddings, rerank, speech to text and text to speech.** go to its matching APIs. They stay in agents’ lists as they are on the remote; being listed doesn’t make them able to hold a conversation.
- **Prices..** Each model costs here what the shared jianmu counts it at (a price set there by hand, else its provider’s list price), so the two computers count the same. A price you set here comes first.

## Quotas and usage

The Usage page, the menu bar and `jianmu quota` show the shared jianmu’s subscription cards, named with it (`Codex · office`, id `office/codex`), as that jianmu last read them: only the computer with the sign-ins asks the vendors. A card’s refresh here has it read that card once more, at most once every 30 seconds. A Codex reset or a WorkBuddy check-in is pressed on that computer, from its own app, TUI or CLI. A key that jianmu holds to a budget, some models or some accounts is told none of its cards: only that key’s own card shows here, with its limit.

The shared jianmu counts this computer’s requests under the name of the gateway key it sends, with the account that answered.

## Short-lived keys

A program that starts agents in sandboxes can give each one a gateway key of its own that stops working by itself. The key lives 1 minute to 30 days, and may be held to some models, some accounts, a number of tokens or a cost over its whole life, or to read-only use. Its secret is told once, in the answer.

```
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/keys \
  -d '{"name":"sandbox-1","ttl":"1h","models":["office/codex/gpt-5"],"tokens":200000}'
# {"id":"k…","name":"sandbox-1","key":"sk-jianmu-…","expires":"…","models":[…],"limit":{…}}
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/keys              # the keys you issued, masked
curl -s -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/keys/k…  # revoke one early
```

A program on this computer may call it with no key; a page in a browser may not. Another computer, a container or CI calls it with a gateway key you let issue keys, and every key it issues is held to that key: never a model or account it may not use, never past its own expiry, and what they spend counts against its limit. Turning it off or removing it stops its keys at once. The same from the command line, which prints the key alone:

```
jianmu gateway-key issue --ttl 1h --name sandbox-1 --models office/codex/gpt-5 --tokens 200000
jianmu gateway-key issuer <id> on    # let a key issue keys
jianmu gateway-key issue --ttl 30m --from <id> --read-only --json
jianmu gateway-key list               # until 10-31 14:00, expired, issued by …
```

An expired key is refused with `401` and why (“the gateway key "sandbox-1" expired at …: ask for a new one”) on every API, from this computer too. It is removed an hour later.

## Keys for GitHub Actions

A GitHub Actions job can get a short-lived key without a gateway key in the repository’s secrets: it trades the OIDC token GitHub gives it. Write a rule naming the repository (and, if you like, the branch, environment or any other claim, exact or with `*`), the gateway key its keys are issued under, and how long they live:

```
jianmu gateway-key issuer <id> on
jianmu gateway-key oidc add --key <id> --repo owner/app --ref refs/heads/main --ttl 1h
# prints the rule id and its audience, jianmu-<rule id>
jianmu gateway-key oidc list
jianmu gateway-key oidc remove <rule id>
```

In the workflow, ask GitHub for a token with the rule’s audience and POST it to `/v1/jianmu/keys/oidc`:

```
permissions:
  id-token: write
steps:
  - name: Get a jianmu key
    run: |
      TOKEN=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \
        "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=jianmu-<rule id>" | jq -r .value)
      KEY=$(curl -s -X POST https://<your jianmu>/v1/jianmu/keys/oidc \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"ttl":"30m"}' | jq -r .key)
      echo "::add-mask::$KEY"
      echo "JIANMU_KEY=$KEY" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
```

The key is issued under the rule’s gateway key and held to it like any other issued key, lives no longer than the rule says, and is named after the repository, branch and run. A token from another repository or branch, an expired one, or one already traded gets `401` and why. The route answers another computer only while jianmu is shared, and refused tokens count against the failed sign-ins it allows. Without a rule nothing is traded.

## Management API

Providers, accounts, gateway keys and account groups can be managed with no hand-edited file, by a key you allow to. Allow it from the command line (not through the API: a key can't give another more than it has):

```
jianmu gateway-key add automation
jianmu gateway-key admin <id> local   # this computer only
jianmu gateway-key admin <id> any     # also from other computers
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/admin/providers -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/admin/gateway-keys/add-key \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d '{"name":"ci"}'
```

It answers the same as the app’s own pages do, under `/v1/jianmu/admin/`: `GET providers`, `POST provider/{save,delete,on,off,name,…}`, `POST keys/…` (a provider’s keys), `GET`/`POST gateway-keys[/{add-key,rename-key,limit-key,models-key,remove-key,…}]`, `GET`/`POST account-groups[/…]`, and `POST signin` with `{"agent":…}`, which answers the vendor’s page and the code to type there, never a password; open it on a computer with a browser. A saved key and a gateway key’s secret are never told again, and what changes this computer’s apps is not served.

A key that is read-only, the extension’s, issued or short-lived, or the sharing key, can’t have it. A web page can’t call it, with a key or without (any request with `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-*` is refused), and nor can a request under another name for this computer. Shared over the network, only a key set to `any` gets in.

## Stats API

What the Usage page shows is also served as JSON, to this computer and, while jianmu is shared, to a request with a gateway key. A key held to a budget, models or accounts is told only its own calls and limit, and the quotas of what it may use once its owner turns on Quotas for it (`jianmu gateway-key quotas <id> on`).

- `/v1/jianmu/usage?period=today|7d|30d|all`: totals, by model, agent, provider, account and gateway key.
- `/v1/jianmu/usage/requests`: the request log, with `period`, `day`, `offset`, `limit`, and filters `model`, `agent`, `provider`, `account`, `callerKey`, `failed=1`, `retried=1` and `q`.
- `/v1/jianmu/quotas`: each subscription’s windows (`?kept=1` without asking the vendors); `/v1/jianmu/quotas/history?days=`: what was left over time, 45 days at most.
- `/v1/jianmu/limit`: the key’s own limits, its expiry, and its issuer’s limits; for a held key, what holds it (`heldTo`), its `models`, and whether it is told quotas (`quotas`, `quotaProviders`).
- `/v1/jianmu/concurrency`: requests in flight, per account.

```
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/usage?period=7d'
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/usage/requests?period=today&callerKey=k…&failed=1&limit=50'
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/quotas?kept=1'
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/quotas/history?days=14'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/limit -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-jianmu-…'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/jianmu/concurrency
```

## When it doesn’t work

| You see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| “jianmu isn’t shared on the local network”, or “remote jianmu isn’t shared” | turn on Share on local network on that computer |
| “remote jianmu didn’t take this key” (401) | use one of its enabled gateway keys: Gateway → Gateway keys there |
| 403 for a model | that key may use only some models: `jianmu gateway-key models <id>` on that computer shows or changes them. A bare `office` asks System One’s first decision model, whatever the key allows; use the full `office/provider/model` id |
| “couldn’t reach the remote jianmu” | check the address, that jianmu is running there with sharing on, and that its firewall lets the port in |
| no System One models, or “doesn’t share its quotas” | update jianmu on that computer, then refresh the list here |

> **Away from home**, reach the shared jianmu over a VPN such as Tailscale or WireGuard, with its address there. Don’t open its port to the internet.

Questions or a setup worth sharing? Ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues). The [reference](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/docs/reference.md) has the details.

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/docker

# jianmu in Docker

Run jianmu on a server or a NAS that has no desktop: its gateway serves your models to agents on other computers, and you add providers and sign in to subscriptions from a page in your browser.

| **Image** | `ghcr.io/DamonZS/Jianmu`, for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` |
| --- | --- |
| **Tags** | `latest` (the newest release), `daily` (the newest release as of 20:00 UTC, moved once a day), `stable` (the desktop app's Stable channel: a release a week, out three days first, or an urgent one at once), `0.1.1150` (one release), `0.1`, `edge` (every change on `main`) |
| **Ports** | `3425` the gateway agents call; `3430` the browser UI, when the container runs `jianmu web`; it answers the gateway’s `/v1` routes too, so a reverse proxy needs only this port |
| **Volume** | `/config`: providers, keys, sign-ins, plugins and usage |
| **User** | nonroot (uid 65532) |

The image holds jianmu’s terminal-only build on Debian 12 slim, with bash for a terminal in the container and curl for the installers of the CLIs some subscriptions sign in with (Cursor, Devin, Grok Build). It runs `jianmu serve` (the gateway alone) unless given another command. The container finds no agents to wire, so jianmu in it is a gateway: the agents that use it run elsewhere.

## Run it

Run it with the browser UI, a key for that page you keep across restarts, and both ports on the host’s loopback only:

```
docker run -d --name jianmu --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 127.0.0.1:3425:3425 -p 127.0.0.1:3430:3430 \
  -e JIANMU_WEB_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \
  -v jianmu-config:/config \
  ghcr.io/DamonZS/Jianmu:latest web --addr 0.0.0.0:3430 --no-open

docker logs jianmu
```

The log names the page with its key:

```
● jianmu web on http://127.0.0.1:3430/?k=0f3c9a1e…
  on the network http://172.17.0.2:3430/?k=0f3c9a1e…
  these are the container's own addresses: other machines use the host's, and JIANMU_PUBLIC_URL=http://<host>:<port> puts it here
  other containers on this host http://172.17.0.1:3425
! anyone with the link can change jianmu and see its keys, and the network carries it unencrypted
  the link carries JIANMU_WEB_KEY · gateway http://127.0.0.1:3425 · Ctrl-C to stop
```

> **Agents outside the container need a gateway key.** In the container any key works. A request from the host or another machine is answered only with an enabled gateway key, and gets 401 without one: make one as in Gateway keys. `127.0.0.1:` in `-p` keeps a port on the host; leave it out, or name the host’s LAN or VPN address, for other machines to reach it.

Without `web --addr 0.0.0.0:3430 --no-open` the container runs the gateway alone, which you then set up from a terminal in it (`docker exec -it jianmu jianmu provider add …`). A folder bind-mounted at `/config` works in place of the named volume, if uid 65532 can write it: `sudo chown -R 65532:65532 /volume1/docker/jianmu/config`.

## The browser UI

Open the link from the log. The key in it is traded for a cookie and taken out of the address; a page opened without it is turned away (401). With `JIANMU_WEB_KEY` set (16 or more letters, digits or `- . _ ~`; `openssl rand -hex 16` makes one) the key stays the same across restarts and the browser stays signed in for 400 days. Without it, every start makes a new key and the cookie lasts the browser session.

The page is in **gateway mode**: Providers, Gateway, Routing, Usage, Sessions, Plugins and Settings, with no Agents, since there are no agents in the container. Library has its MCP servers alone, with the MCP router: other computers’ apps connect at the router’s address with a gateway key. Sessions lists only the sessions of agents on other computers that came through this gateway, never this machine’s agents’ files. Settings → General → Gateway mode turns it off.

On a NAS or a server you reach over SSH, open the page through a tunnel rather than publishing 3430: `ssh -L 3430:127.0.0.1:3430 you@nas`, then the log’s link on your own computer.

> **Anyone with the link can change jianmu and see its keys.** Keep 3430 on loopback or a VPN. Across the network, serve it over HTTPS: give jianmu a certificate with `JIANMU_TLS_CERT` and `JIANMU_TLS_KEY`, or put it behind a reverse proxy with TLS, such as Caddy.

## Sign in to subscriptions

Add API keys on Providers as on the desktop. A subscription’s sign-in (ChatGPT, Claude…) opens the vendor’s page in your browser, and when you are done the vendor sends that browser back to `localhost`, for ChatGPT `http://localhost:1455/auth/callback?code=…`. That is your own computer, not the container, so the page doesn’t load. Copy its whole address from the address bar and paste it into the sign-in’s Callback URL field.

The same from a terminal:

```
docker exec -it jianmu jianmu accounts add codex
```

Open the link it prints, sign in, then paste the address the browser ended on. The browser UI can also import sign-ins from a file.

A Claude subscription is signed in to and answered through Claude Code, which the image doesn’t have. Have jianmu download Anthropic’s own build first: it says the version, where it comes from and where it goes, asks, and checks the download’s SHA-256 against Anthropic’s manifest. It is kept in `/config/cache`, on the volume, so a new image keeps it, and jianmu keeps it at Claude Code’s newest release by itself: it looks a minute after it starts and every six hours, and downloads a newer one the same way. Nothing needs installing again after an update. To hold a version, set `-e DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1`. `jianmu accounts add claude` offers it too when Claude Code is missing.

```
docker exec -it jianmu jianmu claude-code install
```

A Grok (SuperGrok) subscription signs in through xAI’s Grok Build CLI, which the image doesn’t have either. Its sign-in, in the browser UI or with `jianmu plugin login grok`, installs it first, as xAI’s installer does: the stable version from `x.ai/cli`, kept in `/config/home/.grok`. To use a Grok Build binary you put on the volume yourself, set `GROK_BIN_DIR` to the folder holding it.

## Your own browser

Jianmu Browser lets agents act in your own browser, through its extension. The extension can’t be loaded from the container’s folders, so in the browser UI open Library → Jianmu Browser and click Download the extension. The zip is pointed at the page’s own address, with a gateway key named **Jianmu Browser** of its own. Unzip it, open `chrome://extensions`, turn on Developer mode and click Load unpacked on the unzipped folder. An extension already loaded takes the address (`http://localhost:3430`, or the gateway’s published port) and a gateway key in its popup.

The Jianmu Browser key connects the extension and nothing else: it can’t use models, MCP servers or stats, so a copy of the zip left in Downloads spends nothing. The host’s browser reaches the container from Docker’s bridge, not from the container’s own computer, so it is that key’s alone and the container’s agents don’t use it yet ([#5529](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues/5529)). To use it from an agent on the host, give that agent a gateway key of its own with full access, connect the extension with the same key in its popup, and call `/mcp/jianmu/browser` with it. A browser given another key is that key’s alone, and it is let go once its key is turned off, removed or rotated.

## What is kept

Everything jianmu writes is under `/config`, so a restart, or a new container on the same volume, keeps your providers, keys, sign-ins and plugins.

| Path | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `/config/jianmu` | jianmu’s own files: `settings.json`, providers, gateway keys, routing groups |
| `/config/home` | the container’s `HOME`: sign-ins kept where their agent keeps them (`~/.codex`, `~/.claude`…) |
| `/config/cache` | the model catalog, Bun, which plugins run on (downloaded the first time one is used), and the Claude Code `jianmu claude-code install` downloaded |
| `/config/data`, `/config/state` | the rest of what jianmu keeps |

A volume made by an older image keeps working: jianmu adds the folders it lacks when it starts. Only sign-ins made with that older image, which lived outside the volume, have to be made again.

## Environment

| Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `JIANMU_ADDR` | where the gateway listens. The image sets `0.0.0.0:3425`, so the published port reaches it. |
| `JIANMU_PUBLIC_URL` | the address other machines reach the gateway at, such as `http://192.168.1.20:3425` (the host’s or the NAS’s, on the published port), or a reverse proxy’s base URL. In the container jianmu sees only Docker’s own `172.17.x` address; with this set, the address it shows and prints is the one to use. |
| `JIANMU_WEB_KEY` | the browser UI’s key, kept across restarts (16+ characters) |
| `JIANMU_TLS_CERT`, `JIANMU_TLS_KEY` | a PEM certificate (its chain after it) and its key, mounted into the container: other machines then reach the gateway and the browser UI over `https://` only, and plain HTTP from them gets 400. The files are read again when they change, so a renewal needs no restart. One without the other, or files that don’t load, stop jianmu from starting. Use `https://` in `JIANMU_PUBLIC_URL` too. |
| `JIANMU_ALLOW_IPS` | the only addresses other machines may reach the gateway and the browser UI from, as IPs and CIDR ranges: `203.0.113.7,10.0.0.0/8,2001:db8::/32`. Any other address gets 403, even with a gateway key. Unset lets every address in, each with a key. See Allowed addresses. |
| `HOME`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME` | set by the image to the folders under `/config` above; leave them |

## Gateway keys and other machines

1. **Make a key for each client.** Gateway → Gateway keys, or in a terminal `docker exec jianmu jianmu gateway-key add "Laptop"`, which prints the new `sk-jianmu-key-…`. Every request from outside the container, the host’s own included, must carry an enabled gateway key, and one without gets 401. A key can have its own daily, weekly, monthly, every-N-days or every-N-hours limit and its own list of models (`jianmu gateway-key limit`, `jianmu gateway-key models`).
2. **Publish the port.** Recreate the container with `-p 3425:3425`, or bound to the NAS’s LAN or VPN address (`-p 192.168.1.20:3425:3425`), and with `-e JIANMU_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.20:3425`.

On each other computer, point the agent at the gateway with one of those keys as its API key: `http://192.168.1.20:3425/v1` for an OpenAI client, `http://192.168.1.20:3425` for an Anthropic or Gemini one. Model ids are `provider/model`, or a routing group’s; `GET /v1/models` lists them. If that computer runs jianmu itself, add the container as a [Remote jianmu](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/remote) instead, and jianmu wires its agents for you.

**Other containers on the same host.** Another container on the NAS reaches jianmu at the host, through the Docker bridge’s gateway and the published port: `http://172.17.0.1:3425` on Docker’s default bridge. The container’s own `172.17.x` address is no use to it, and the host’s LAN address may not be either, as a NAS’s firewall can keep containers from it. `host.docker.internal` is the same address on Docker Desktop, and on Linux only in a container given `extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]`. A container on jianmu’s own compose network, or one you made, can use its name, `http://jianmu:3425`. Either way it sends a gateway key. The log and the browser UI list this address as Other containers on this host, after the host’s address the page was opened at.

Settings → Network and sharing → Share on local network isn’t needed in the container: turning it on also makes a gateway key named Jianmu, and the gateway asks for a key from outside the container either way.

**Upgrading from an earlier image.** An agent outside the container that sends `jianmu`, or any other key that isn’t an enabled gateway key, now gets 401 (“the API key sent is not an enabled jianmu gateway key”). Make it a key as above and put that in the agent’s settings. Agents that already send a gateway key, and a Remote jianmu set up with one, keep working.

**Allowed addresses.** On a public host, set `-e JIANMU_ALLOW_IPS=203.0.113.7,10.0.0.0/8` to the addresses your clients come from. A request from any other address is refused 403 before its key is looked at, so a key that leaks is no use from elsewhere; the refusal names the address it came from, as does the container’s log. jianmu judges the address of the connection itself, never an `X-Forwarded-For` header, and a mistyped entry lets nothing in rather than everything. Docker’s default bridge network passes a client’s own address into the container, but a request from the host itself arrives from the bridge’s gateway (`172.17.0.1`), and Docker Desktop and rootless Docker show every client as one address of their own: add that, or check what the 403 says. Behind a reverse proxy or tunnel, every request comes from the proxy’s address, so limit who reaches jianmu at the proxy. On the desktop app the same list is Settings → Network and sharing → Allowed addresses.

> **Over the internet, prefer a VPN** such as Tailscale or WireGuard to opening 3425. A reverse proxy or tunnel in front of the container is the network too: its clients need a gateway key like any other machine’s.

**Claude Code’s status line, with Claude Code outside the container.** The status line square can’t reach another machine’s `~/.claude/settings.json`, and the command it writes names a binary in the container. The gateway answers the same line itself: on the machine Claude Code runs on, set `statusLine` in `~/.claude/settings.json` to `{"type": "command", "command": "curl -fsS -m 1 -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-jianmu-key-…' --data-binary @- http://<host>:3425/v1/jianmu/statusline || true"}`, with the host or address that reaches the container and a gateway key (a read-only key is enough). A key held to a budget, models or accounts gets the line once its owner turns on Quotas for it, with only the accounts it may use. Add `?format=json` for the same as JSON (the line, the model, and each account’s windows with `used` and `resetsAt`), for a status line that draws its own. Claude Code runs it on every message and passes its session on stdin, which adds the model the session went to. The same command is shown in the browser UI under Settings → About.

## Docker Compose on a NAS

```
services:
  jianmu:
    image: ghcr.io/DamonZS/Jianmu:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # 127.0.0.1: the host alone; every caller outside the container needs a gateway key
      - "127.0.0.1:3425:3425"
      - "127.0.0.1:3430:3430"
    environment:
      JIANMU_PUBLIC_URL: http://<nas-address>:3425
      JIANMU_WEB_KEY: <random-key>
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config
    command: [web, --addr, 0.0.0.0:3430, --no-open]
```

Then: `sudo chown -R 65532:65532 ./config`, `docker compose up -d`, open `http://127.0.0.1:3430/?k=<random-key>` through an SSH tunnel, add your providers and make a gateway key for each machine. For other machines to reach the gateway, change its line to `"3425:3425"` (or the NAS’s LAN or VPN address) and run `docker compose up -d` again.

## Health, terminal, updates

- **Health..** The image has a `HEALTHCHECK`: `jianmu healthcheck` exits 0 while the gateway answers, under `serve` and `web` alike, so `docker ps` shows the container as healthy and Compose can wait for it with `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`.
- **Terminal..** `docker exec -it jianmu bash`, or a NAS panel’s terminal, opens a shell with `jianmu` on its PATH: `jianmu providers`, `jianmu models`, `jianmu usage`, `jianmu quota` and the rest of the [CLI](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/docs/reference.md).
- **Updates..** Pull the new image and recreate the container on the same volume: `docker pull ghcr.io/DamonZS/Jianmu:latest`, then `docker rm -f jianmu` and the same `docker run`, or `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`. jianmu releases several times a day; for one update a day with Renovate or Watchtower, follow `daily` (with Renovate, pin its digest), or `stable` for one a week.
- **Build it yourself..** `docker build -t jianmu .` in a checkout of [the repository](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu) makes the same image.

Questions or a setup worth sharing? Ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues). The [reference](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/docs/reference.md#docker) has the details.

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/import

# Add to jianmu

Hand your users one link, and your models show up in every agent they run: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Pi, Crush. No config files, no environment variables, no copy-pasting base URLs.

## Quick start

1. **Build a link.** Describe your endpoint as URL parameters: a name, a base URL per API you speak, and optionally the user’s key and the models to offer.
2. **Put it behind a button.** On your dashboard, next to the key you just minted: *Add to jianmu*.
3. **The user confirms.** jianmu opens, shows exactly where prompts and the key will go, and adds the provider when the user says yes. Every agent can use it right away.

```
https://usejianmu.ai/import#name=Acme%20Relay&chat=https://api.acme.example/v1&anthropic=https://api.acme.example&key=sk-…&models=gpt-5.5,claude-sonnet-5
```

## The link

jianmu registers the `jianmu://` scheme with the system. An import link is that scheme, the word `import`, and a query string:

On the web, link to the same parameters on `usejianmu.ai/import` instead, after a `#`:

### Why the https link

It works everywhere a link does: GitHub READMEs, chat apps and email clients drop or block custom schemes. It opens jianmu, and offers the download when jianmu isn’t installed yet.

### Why after the `#`

Browsers never send the fragment to a server. The key goes from your page to the user’s machine without passing through usejianmu.ai, not even its logs.

Every value is URL-encoded, as `URLSearchParams` or `urlencode` produce. Both `%20` and `+` work for spaces.

## Parameters

A link either names one of jianmu’s presets, which already knows the vendor’s endpoints, or describes a provider from scratch with a name and at least one base URL.

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name`or preset | What the provider is called in jianmu, at most 80 characters. |
| `chat` | OpenAI Chat Completions base URL, ending in `/v1` (jianmu appends `/chat/completions`). |
| `responses` | OpenAI Responses base URL, ending in `/v1`. Codex speaks only this API; jianmu translates for it when you don’t. |
| `anthropic` | Anthropic Messages base URL: the root, without `/v1`. |
| `gemini` | Google Gemini API base URL, ending in `/v1beta`, as the app’s editor and the TUI take one. |
| `key` | The user’s API key. Leave it out and the user pastes one in the dialog. |
| `models` | Model ids to offer the agents, comma separated. Without it, jianmu lists the models your `/v1/models` returns. |
| `id` | The id agents use in `id/model`. Defaults to the name, lowercased with dashes (`Acme Relay` → `acme-relay`). |
| `catalog` | A [models.dev](https://models.dev) provider id whose metadata applies, e.g. `openai` for a relay of OpenAI models: display names, context sizes (written into the agents that take them), reasoning levels and image input; the model list when the provider’s own `/models` can’t be read; and per-token prices, which the Usage page turns into a cost estimate in USD. Several ids may be given, comma-separated: their models are combined, and where two know the same model the first one’s entry is used. |
| `website` | Your site (https). Shown on the provider’s page. |
| `keys` | The page where users make keys (https). The dialog links to it when the link has no key. |
| `icon` | A picture of your own (https): PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, ICO or SVG, at most 1 MB. jianmu downloads it once, after the user confirms the import, and keeps it beside the provider. Without one, jianmu shows the `catalog` vendor’s logo or a plain mark. |
| `balance` | Where the key’s balance is read (https), on the host of one of your base URLs: jianmu asks it with the key, as a chat request sends it. `{key}` in it stands for the key. Without it, jianmu reads the vendors it knows, and asks a relay where new-api and sub2api tell a key its balance (`/api/usage/token`, `/v1/usage`); give one when yours answers elsewhere. |
| `balance_path` | Where the amount is in the JSON reply: a dotted path, list items by index (`data.balance`, `balance_infos.0.total_balance`), or a sum of them in your own units (`$ data.quota / 500000`). `$` or `¥` before it is the currency, `%` after it a percent of 1; several amounts go apart by `;`, each with a `label:` if wanted. Needs `balance`. |
| `balance_method` | `GET`, the default, or `POST` with no body. Needs `balance`. |
| `preset`or name | A preset id; its endpoints, catalog and pages are used, and `name` may rename it. |
| `region` | With a preset that has regions, which one. |

At least one of `chat`, `responses`, `anthropic` and `gemini` is required without a preset; give every API you speak, and each agent uses the one it speaks natively. Base URLs must be **https**, except plain http to `localhost`, loopback, private addresses and `*.local`, where model servers usually run without TLS. They can’t carry a query, a fragment or credentials.

A link sets no other header or token for the balance: an account-wide access token is worth more than one key, and a URL stays in browser history. A balance that needs one is set up in the provider’s editor.

### Presets

Vendors jianmu already knows. `jianmu presets` prints the current list.

A vendor with a preset only needs to add the key: `jianmu://import?preset=deepseek&key=sk-…`. Want yours on the list? [Open an issue](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

## Link builder

Fill in your endpoint; the link, the button and the Markdown follow as you type. Everything stays in this page.

## The button

Two ready-made badges, one for light pages and one for dark. Link them to your import link, or draw your own button: the words *Add to jianmu* and the bird are yours to use.

```
<a href="https://usejianmu.ai/import#preset=deepseek&key=sk-…">
  <img src="https://usejianmu.ai/img/add-to-jianmu.svg" alt="Add to jianmu" width="176" height="40">
</a>
```

```
[![Add to jianmu](https://usejianmu.ai/img/add-to-jianmu.svg)](https://usejianmu.ai/import#preset=deepseek)
```

For dark pages, use `add-to-jianmu-light.svg`. A public page like a README should never carry a key; leave `key` out and the user pastes their own.

## From your backend

The natural place for the button is the page that shows a freshly minted key. Build the link where you have it:

```
const params = new URLSearchParams({
  name: "Acme Relay",
  chat: "https://api.acme.example/v1",
  anthropic: "https://api.acme.example",
  key: apiKey,
  models: ["gpt-5.5", "claude-sonnet-5"].join(","),
  icon: "https://acme.example/logo.svg",
});
const href = "https://usejianmu.ai/import#" + params;
```

```
from urllib.parse import urlencode

href = "https://usejianmu.ai/import#" + urlencode({
    "name": "Acme Relay",
    "chat": "https://api.acme.example/v1",
    "anthropic": "https://api.acme.example",
    "key": api_key,
    "models": "gpt-5.5,claude-sonnet-5",
    "icon": "https://acme.example/logo.svg",
})
```

```
jianmu import 'jianmu://import?preset=deepseek&key=sk-…'   # asks first; -y to skip
```

## Security

An import link is a suggestion. The user decides.

- **Always confirmed..** jianmu shows the name, every host that prompts and the key will go to, and the models, and saves nothing until the user presses Add. The user can rename it, or replace the key, first.
- **No silent overwrites..** When the id is already taken, the dialog says so and the button reads *Replace*.
- **https only..** Plain http is refused except to this machine or the local network; `file:`, credentials in URLs and other schemes are refused outright.
- **Read once..** Inside the app, the link’s contents are handed to the window a single time; a reload doesn’t bring the dialog back.
- **Icons are fetched, not embedded..** An `icon=` URL is downloaded by jianmu, only after the user confirms the import, only over https, and only into its own icons folder — at most 1 MB, and the type is checked. jianmu asks for it through usejianmu.ai’s icon proxy, so your host sees Cloudflare’s address and never the user’s, and the fetch is made from Cloudflare, where nothing on the user’s own machine or network can be reached. A loopback or local-network name is refused before anything is asked. The page and the dialog never load a remote picture directly.
- **The balance stays on your hosts..** A `balance=` URL on any host but one of the link’s base URLs is refused, so the key goes nowhere its requests don’t already go. It is asked only after the user adds the provider.
- **Keys stay out of servers..** The web link keeps parameters in the fragment. The key ends up only in `~/.config/jianmu/providers.json`, readable by the user alone.

## Platforms

| System | How `jianmu://` gets registered |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | By the app itself, as soon as jianmu.app is in Applications. |
| Windows | For the current user, the first time jianmu runs. |
| Linux | By a desktop entry (`x-scheme-handler/jianmu`), written by the installer and again on first run. |
| Terminal | `jianmu import <link>` shows the same summary and asks before adding. |

Import links need jianmu 0.1.8 or later. When jianmu is already running, the link goes to that instance and its window comes forward.

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/integrate

# Integrate your app

For developers of an AI app, agent or client who want it to work well with jianmu. There are three levels, from no work on jianmu’s side to a row of your own on the Agents page.

| You want | Route | Change to jianmu |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your app’s requests served by jianmu, counted under its own name in Usage | Talk to the gateway | none |
| A row on the Agents page: detected, its model picked there, put back on disconnect | An agent adapter | a pull request |
| A new model source (a subscription, a vendor), or rewriting requests | A plugin | none |

## 1. Talk to the gateway

jianmu runs a local LLM gateway. Every model the user has in jianmu (subscriptions, API keys, local models, routing groups) is served there under one id each, so your app needs one provider entry, not one per vendor.

### Find it

The gateway listens on `127.0.0.1:3425`, or on the port in `port` of jianmu’s `settings.json` (`~/.config/jianmu/settings.json`, the same path under the user’s folder on Windows; `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jianmu` when that is set). `GET /api/hello` answers `{"name":"jianmu","version":"…"}` when it is jianmu. Read that file, never write it. jianmu must be running (the app or `jianmu serve`); an app that finds nothing there offers its own providers as usual.

```
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/api/hello
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer jianmu-acme"
```

### Endpoints

Requests go straight through when the vendor speaks your API, and are translated otherwise, streaming, tool calls, images and reasoning included. The base URL is `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/v1` for an OpenAI client and `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` for an Anthropic or Gemini one.

| Path | API |
| --- | --- |
| `/v1/chat/completions` | OpenAI Chat Completions |
| `/v1/responses` | OpenAI Responses |
| `/v1/messages`, `/v1/messages/count_tokens` | Anthropic Messages |
| `/v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent` (and `:streamGenerateContent`) | Google Gemini |
| `/v1/models` | the catalog |
| `/api/version`, `/api/tags`, `/api/show` | the catalog as an Ollama server lists it, for a client that takes only an Ollama endpoint (Copilot in Visual Studio and VS Code: enter `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` as the Ollama URL; it chats on `/v1/chat/completions`, and `/api/chat` isn’t served) |

### The key names your app

On this machine the gateway takes any key. Send `jianmu-<your-app-id>` (`Authorization: Bearer jianmu-acme`, or `x-api-key`) and every call is counted as `acme` in Usage, the Requests log and the routing rules that match on agents. Without it, jianmu counts the call by the first word of your `User-Agent` (`Acme/1.4 (darwin)` is `Acme`); an SDK’s own User-Agent (`OpenAI/JS …`, `ai-sdk/…`) would count it as that SDK. From another computer (Settings → Share on local network) the key must be one of the user’s gateway keys, and the User-Agent names your app.

### Models

`GET /v1/models` lists what the user has turned on: `id` (`provider/model`, or a routing group’s name, sent as it is), `display_name`, `owned_by` (the provider), `reasoning` and `supported_reasoning_levels` (`[{"effort":"low"},…]`, and the same as plain names in `reasoning_levels`), `context_window` and `max_output_tokens` when known, and `modalities` when jianmu knows whether it takes images. List them from there rather than shipping a list: the user adds and removes providers in jianmu. Reasoning is asked in your API’s own field (`reasoning_effort`, `reasoning.effort`, Anthropic’s `thinking` or `output_config.effort`). `?format=text` gives the ids one a line. The list holds chat models alone: ask for image and video models with `?kind=image,video` (or `?kind=all`). Each is marked `"kind": "image"` or `"video"` and is made on `/v1/images/generations` or `/v1/videos`, not a chat route.

A vendor’s own fields: `/v1/images/generations` and `/v1/videos` take OpenAI’s fields and pass the others on to a vendor that takes them, such as Volcengine Ark’s `content` (reference video and audio, `draft_task`), `ratio`, `resolution`, `duration: -1`, `tools`, `watermark` and `sequential_image_generation`, and a video’s answer carries Ark’s own fields (`content.last_frame_url`, `usage`). For the rest of a vendor’s API use `/v1/jianmu/native/<provider>/<path>`: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`, with `<path>` joined to the provider’s host (not its base URL), in the vendor’s own shape on the user’s key for that provider, a stream as it comes; Ark’s task list is `GET /v1/jianmu/native/ark/api/v3/contents/generations/tasks`. It serves a provider added with an API key, not a subscription or sign-in, and Ark’s short paths (`images/generations`, `contents/generations/tasks`) still work under the key’s base. It takes the same gateway key as every route, and a key held to models, accounts or a budget is refused it.

### Optional

Send `X-Magpie-Session: <id>` with a conversation’s requests and `GET /v1/jianmu/route?session=<id>` says which model a routing group picked for the turn and the fallbacks it tried, before the first token (long-poll with `after=<seq>&wait=<s>`). `GET /v1/jianmu/quotas` lists the user’s subscription allowances, and `GET /v1/jianmu/usage` and `/v1/jianmu/usage/requests` the Usage page’s numbers and its requests (with `session`, and `subagent`/`parent_agent` for a Claude Code subagent’s call). They answer only this machine, or another with a gateway key; a key held to a budget, models or accounts sees its own calls and routes alone, and is refused the quotas unless its owner lets it see those of what it may use (`jianmu gateway-key quotas <id> on`; its own limit is `GET /v1/jianmu/limit`). Calls your app makes to its vendor itself can be reported with `POST /v1/jianmu/usage/requests` (one record or up to 5000 a post, in `usage.jsonl`’s shape, each with a `rid`; past times are kept, so a history can be backfilled). They show on the Usage page as reported, and never count against a key’s limit. The [reference](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/docs/reference.md#connecting-anything-else) has the details.

> **Keep the user’s providers.** Add jianmu as one more provider (named Jianmu) beside the ones the user set up in your app, rather than replacing them, so turning jianmu off is picking another provider.

## 2. A row on the Agents page

The agents jianmu lists (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, dsh, Alma, Cindy…) are adapters in [`internal/agent`](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/tree/main/internal/agent), one file each. A row gets your app’s name and icon, shows when your app is installed, lets the user pick its model (and reasoning) from jianmu’s catalog, follows the catalog as providers change, and on disconnect puts back what your app had before. There is no runtime registration: a row is added by a pull request to jianmu, and ships in the next release.

An adapter is an [`Agent`](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/internal/agent/agent.go) value. What your app offers decides its shape:

- **jianmu edits your config file.** (most adapters; [`fx.go`](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/internal/agent/fx.go), [`empryo.go`](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/internal/agent/empryo.go)). `Dir`, `Path` and `Bin` find the app; each `Field` (`model`, `effort`…) has `Get`, `Set` and `Options`. Connecting adds a `jianmu` provider at the gateway, keyed `jianmu-<id>`, and sets your model to one of jianmu’s; the agent’s default or `Unwire` takes jianmu’s entries out and restores what was there. Only the keys jianmu sets are touched. `Notice` says when your app must be restarted; `Sync` rewrites a model list your app keeps in a file.
- **Your app takes a provider only through its own import link, confirmed in your app.** ([`cindy.go`](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/blob/main/internal/agent/cindy.go)). `Import` returns the link (`yourapp://provider/import?…` with the gateway’s URL, the key `jianmu-<id>` and the endpoints), the row’s button opens it, and the user says yes once, in your app. `Added` reads, read-only, whether your app has jianmu already. jianmu writes nothing of yours. This suits an app that keeps its providers in a database or encrypted.
- **Your app has a local API while it runs.** (Alma, Shelley): jianmu adds itself as a provider and sets the default model through it.

A pull request needs the adapter and its entry in `agents.go`, `UA` (what your User-Agent begins with, lower-case) so Usage knows your calls, an icon in `internal/gui/assets/icons`, tests that run under a temporary `HOME` (connect, switch, disconnect restoring the original file), and a row in the reference’s Agents table. What helps most is a stable, documented config format or import link, and where your app keeps it on each system.

## 3. Plugins

A plugin is an npm package jianmu runs; the user installs it from Settings → Plugins or with `jianmu plugin add <package>`. **Provider plugins** (OpenCode’s `auth` hook, or a pi package) add a source of models, such as a subscription jianmu doesn’t sign in to itself. **Gateway middleware** rewrites requests and replies as they pass. See the [plugin guide](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/plugins). A plugin can’t add a row to the Agents page or write another app’s config, so it is not how an app registers itself.

## What isn’t there

- No API or link lets another app register itself as an agent, or install a plugin, without the user: plugins are installed in jianmu by the user, and agent rows come from adapters in jianmu’s source.
- `jianmu://import` links add a *provider* (a source of models, with its key), not an agent or an app: see [Add to jianmu](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/import).

Questions, or an adapter you’d like to discuss first: open an [issue](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues) or ask on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/DamonZS/Jianmu/issues).

---

Source: https://usejianmu.ai/docs/plugins

# Writing a plugin

A plugin signs in to a service and makes its requests. jianmu turns it into a provider that every agent can use, with several accounts, failover, usage and the rest. jianmu runs [OpenCode’s provider plugins](https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/), so a plugin written for OpenCode works here unchanged, and it runs [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi)’s packages that register a provider too (see pi packages). This page covers what a plugin author needs: the hooks jianmu calls, what it does with their answers, and how to test, publish and list a plugin.

> **In one paragraph.** A plugin is an npm package, a git repository or a folder. Its module exports an async function in OpenCode’s v1 plugin shape. jianmu loads every plugin into one [Bun](https://bun.sh) process, the *plugin host*. The function returns hooks: `config` declares the provider and its default models. `auth` gives the sign-in methods, plus a `loader` whose `fetch` makes each request. `provider.models` lists the models one account has. `auth.usage` says how much of the plan is used. It is jianmu’s own hook, and OpenCode ignores it. `auth.refresh` renews an account’s token before it runs out, once at a time. It is jianmu’s own hook too. `auth.checkin` presses the vendor’s daily check-in for an account. It is jianmu’s own hook too. An agent can send in any API. The gateway translates the request into the API the model speaks (chat completions, Responses, Anthropic Messages or Gemini), hands it to the plugin’s `fetch`, and streams the answer back.

## A plugin in five minutes

This example signs in to Acme, a made-up coding plan. Acme takes an API key, has an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and reports each account’s models and usage. A real plugin differs mainly in how it signs in and signs its requests. This whole example was run against jianmu v0.1.676 and a local stand-in for Acme’s API.

```
{
  "name": "opencode-acme-auth",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "OpenCode provider plugin: Acme Coding Plan",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "./index.mjs",
  "files": ["index.mjs", "README.md"],
  "keywords": ["opencode", "opencode-plugin", "acme"],
  "license": "MIT",
  "jianmu": { "maxConcurrency": 4 }
}
```

```
const PROVIDER = "acme"
const BASE = "https://api.acme.example/v1"

export const AcmeAuthPlugin = async ({ client }) => ({
  // the provider and the models it has before anyone signs in
  config: async (cfg) => {
    cfg.provider ??= {}
    cfg.provider[PROVIDER] ??= {
      name: "Acme",
      npm: "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible", // chat completions
      api: BASE,
      models: {
        "acme-coder": { name: "Acme Coder", limit: { context: 200000, output: 32000 }, tool_call: true },
      },
    }
  },

  auth: {
    provider: PROVIDER,
    methods: [{ type: "api", label: "Acme API key", placeholder: "acme-…" }],
    // what every request of this account is sent with
    async loader(getAuth) {
      const auth = await getAuth()
      if (auth?.type !== "api") return {}
      return {
        baseURL: BASE,
        async fetch(input, init) {
          const headers = new Headers(init?.headers)
          headers.set("authorization", `Bearer ${auth.key}`)
          headers.set("x-acme-client", "opencode-acme-auth/0.1.0")
          return fetch(input, { ...init, headers })
        },
      }
    },
    // jianmu's own hook: how much of the plan is used
    async usage(getAuth) {
      const auth = await getAuth()
      const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/usage`, { headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${auth.key}` } })
      if (!res.ok) return { error: `Acme answered ${res.status}`, windows: [] }
      const u = await res.json()
      return {
        plan: u.plan,
        windows: [{ name: "5 hours", used: u.percent, resetsAt: u.resets_at, span: 5 * 3600 }],
      }
    },
  },

  // the models this account has, asked of Acme
  provider: {
    id: PROVIDER,
    async models(provider, { auth } = {}) {
      if (auth?.type !== "api") return provider.models
      const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/models`, { headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${auth.key}` } })
      if (!res.ok) return provider.models // jianmu keeps the list it had
      const { data } = await res.json()
      const base = provider.models["acme-coder"]
      return Object.fromEntries(data.map((m) => [m.id, { ...base, id: m.id, name: m.name ?? m.id }]))
    },
  },
})
```

Add the folder to jianmu, sign in, and try it:

```
jianmu plugin add ./opencode-acme-auth   # a folder is loaded where it is; nothing is installed
jianmu plugin login acme                 # asks for the key
jianmu plugin                            # acme (Acme, 2 models)  signed in
jianmu provider test acme                # ✓ chat  7 ms · acme-coder
jianmu quota                             # acme · Pro · 5h 37% ↻59m
```

Agents now reach its models as `acme/acme-coder`, the same way as any other provider’s. In the app, open Plugins, click Add a plugin and give it the folder. Then sign in from the provider’s row.

> **Try it in a sandbox.** A plugin you are writing should never touch your real jianmu. Run jianmu with a `HOME` of its own, as Testing shows.

## How jianmu runs plugins

- **Bun..** jianmu downloads Bun the first time a plugin is added, and runs every plugin on it. Bun runs TypeScript as is, so an entry can be `index.ts`.
- **One host process..** Every plugin that is on loads into one Bun process, started the first time one is needed. jianmu and the host talk over stdin and stdout, one JSON message a line. Anything a plugin prints, `console.log` and `process.stdout` included, is sent to stderr. jianmu logs it as `plugin: …`.
- **Installing..** An npm package is installed with `bun add`, with its install scripts left unrun, as OpenCode installs plugins. A dependency that needs a `postinstall` build won’t work.
- Packages come from the npm registry you already use: the `registry=` in your `~/.npmrc`, `install.registry` in `~/.bunfig.toml`, or `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY` / `BUN_CONFIG_REGISTRY` in your shell, before the Mirrors in China switch. A token your `.npmrc` keeps for that registry is sent to it alone. To use another, change npm registry on Plugins → Discover, or run `jianmu plugin registry <url>` (`default` goes back).
- A git repository is fetched by Bun: `github:owner/repo[#ref]`, `git+https://…` or `owner/repo`.
- A path to a folder or file is loaded where it is.

- The community’s packages (`@magpie-community/*`) update by themselves a little after jianmu starts, then every hour.
- Any other package with a newer version shows a dot on Plugins, and in the sidebar Installed reads “1 update”. Plugins then opens on Installed, which names the plugins with a newer version at the top beside Update all; the user updates them with a click or `jianmu plugin update`.
- A spec pinned to a version (`name@1.2.3`) stays on it until the user updates it: Update to …, Update all and `jianmu plugin update` install the newest version and unpin it.
- A git repository has no version to compare. It shows an update when its branch or tag (the default branch without `#ref`) is at another commit than the one Bun installed: GitHub is asked through its API, any other host with `git ls-remote`, at most every ten minutes, and the hourly check asks again. A spec pinned to a commit never has one. The row shows the commit installed.

What jianmu keeps, in its config folder (`~/.config/jianmu`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jianmu`):

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `plugins.json` | The plugins added: `{"plugins": [{"spec", "off"?, "options"?}], "config"?}`. `options` is the plugin’s second argument, as OpenCode’s `["name", {…}]` gives it. `config` is the OpenCode config the plugins are handed. |
| `plugins/` | The installed npm and git packages, a Bun project of their own. |
| `plugin-auth.json` | The sign-ins (mode 600), in the same shape as OpenCode’s `auth.json`, so a sign-in can be moved between the two. |
| `plugin-providers.json` | The providers and models the plugins listed last, so jianmu can start without asking them. |

## The package

### Where jianmu loads it from

jianmu looks for the server side of a plugin in the same places OpenCode does, and loads the first file that exports a plugin:

1. `exports["./server"]`, then `main`, then `exports["."]` (or `exports` when it is a string), in `package.json`.
2. Otherwise `index.ts`, `index.tsx`, `index.js`, `index.mjs` or `index.cjs`.

A path to a single file loads that file.

### What the module exports

- `export default { id, server }` (OpenCode v1): `server` is the plugin.
- Otherwise, **every function the module exports** is called as a plugin, as is every exported `{ server }` object.

So don’t export helper functions from the entry file. Put what your tests need on an object instead, as the community plugins do with `export const _internal = { … }`.

### The function

```
async (input, options) => hooks
// input:   { client, project, directory, worktree, serverUrl, $, experimental_workspace }
// options: the entry's "options" in plugins.json, else undefined
// hooks:   { config?, auth?, provider?, "chat.headers"? }
```

A plugin may return more than one provider by exporting more than one function. Each one’s hooks are separate. When two plugins have an `auth` hook for the same provider, the one loaded last wins, as in OpenCode.

### jianmu’s fields in package.json

OpenCode ignores the `jianmu` object, so these are safe to add to an OpenCode plugin.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `jianmu.icon` | The plugin’s picture, on its card in Discover (read from npm, or from the repository for one on GitHub) and its row in Installed, and the picture of each of its providers that doesn’t give its own: an `https://` URL or a `data:image/…` URI, at most 1 MB. SVG, PNG and the like. |
| `jianmu.name` | The plugin’s name on its row in Installed, and on its sidebar tab when its page gives no title, for a plugin the community’s list doesn’t name (the list’s name wins). The package’s npm name has to be ASCII, so a name like 华为云 HUAWEI goes here. One line, at most 80 bytes; anything else is ignored. It is never shown as reviewed, and never used to find a plugin by name. A repository tagged `jianmu-plugin` shows it on its card under Discover → Unofficial, on GitHub too, in place of the repository’s name. |
| `jianmu.summary` | Its card’s line under Discover → Unofficial, on GitHub, by language: `{ "en": "…", "zh": "…" }`, in the window’s language (zh-TW reads `zh`), else English, else GitHub’s description. One line of at most 300 bytes a language; anything else is ignored. A card showing a name or summary of the package’s own says “Its own words”: nobody reviewed them. |
| `jianmu.maxConcurrency` | How many requests each account takes at once, a whole number from 1 to 1000. A limit the user sets on the provider wins over it. |

The same fields can be set on the `auth` hook (`auth.icon`, `auth.maxConcurrency`), where they win over `package.json`. A plugin that signs in to several providers can give each its own `auth.icon` and keep `jianmu.icon` for the plugin itself.

## Provider and models

### Declaring the provider

The provider’s id is `auth.provider`. If [models.dev](https://models.dev) lists that id, jianmu starts from its entry, as OpenCode does. Otherwise, declare the provider in a `config` hook. Use `??=`, so a provider the user configured in `plugins.json` isn’t written over:

```
config: async (cfg) => {
  cfg.provider ??= {}
  cfg.provider["acme"] ??= {
    name: "Acme",
    npm: "@ai-sdk/anthropic",          // the API its models speak (table below)
    api: "https://api.acme.example/v1", // where requests go, unless the loader says otherwise
    models: {
      "acme-large": {
        name: "Acme Large",
        id: "acme-large-2026-09",          // the id the API takes, when it isn't the key
        limit: { context: 400000, output: 64000 },
        reasoning: true,
        tool_call: true,
        modalities: { input: ["text", "image"] },
        cost: { input: 3, output: 15, cache_read: 0.3 }, // US$ per million tokens; leave out for a plan
        variants: { low: {}, medium: {}, high: {} },        // reasoning levels
      },
    },
  }
}
```

A model can also say `provider: { npm, api }` to use another API or address than the provider’s, `headers`, `options`, and `disabled: true` to hide it.

### In front of a vendor jianmu knows

When the provider’s `api` is the API of a vendor jianmu has a preset for (`https://api.mistral.ai/v1`, `https://api.deepseek.com/v1`, `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`, …), jianmu shapes requests to your provider as it does for that vendor before they reach your `fetch`: Mistral’s thinking parts in place of `reasoning_content`, DeepSeek’s and xAI’s schema rules, OpenRouter’s free pool, and the rest. There is nothing to add; the base URL you already give is what it reads, even when your loader’s `baseURL` sends elsewhere. A base on no preset’s host, on `localhost` or on your network gets no vendor’s handling.

### An upstream that searches the web

When your plugin sits in front of Anthropic’s or OpenAI’s own API, which runs the hosted web search tool itself, set `searches: true` on the provider in the `config` hook. A client’s web search (Claude Code’s WebSearch, Codex’s `web_search`) then reaches your `fetch` as it was sent, on the provider’s Anthropic or Responses models, rather than going through jianmu’s own search. Its Chat models are unaffected. jianmu doesn’t search with it for other models by itself, but it can be named as the searcher in Settings.

### A decision API (System One)

A plugin can serve TypeSafe’s System One API for its provider, so its models can be a [routing group’s classifier](https://usejianmu.ai/docs/intent). Set `decide: true` on the provider in the `config` hook, and `decides: true` on each model that answers questions rather than a conversation, in the `config` hook or on the `models` hook’s list. jianmu then posts each question as `POST {baseURL}/systemone` through your loader’s `fetch`, with the account’s sign-in, as it sends any other request. The body is `{"model", "questions", "state"}`; answer `{"model", "answers": {"<question>": {"choice", "score", "confidence"}}}`.

A marked model, and one named `jev-*`, is offered as a classifier and kept from agents: a chat request to it is refused. Without `decide: true` on the provider, `decides` is ignored and every model stays one to chat with.

### The API a model speaks

The AI SDK package named by `npm`, on the model or on the provider, decides the API. That decides the shape of the request your `fetch` receives. Whatever the agent sent, jianmu’s gateway has already translated it:

| npm | API | Path after the base |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@ai-sdk/anthropic`, `@ai-sdk/google-vertex/anthropic` | Anthropic Messages | `/messages` |
| `@ai-sdk/openai`, `@ai-sdk/azure` | OpenAI Responses | `/responses` |
| `@ai-sdk/google` | Gemini | `/models/<id>:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse` |
| `@ai-sdk/github-copilot` | Responses for GPT-5 and later (not gpt-5-mini), chat completions for the rest | `/responses` or `/chat/completions` |
| anything else (`@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`, `xai`, `groq`, `deepseek`, …) | Chat completions | `/chat/completions` |

The base is chosen in this order:

1. the loader’s `baseURL`;
2. the model’s `provider.api`;
3. the provider’s `api`;
4. the AI SDK package’s own default (`https://api.anthropic.com/v1`, `https://api.openai.com/v1`, …).

The body’s `model` is the model’s API id: its `id`, else its key.

### Each account’s models

When the models depend on the account, add a `provider` hook:

```
provider: {
  id: "acme",
  async models(provider, { auth }) {
    // provider.models: what models.dev and the config hook give, keyed by id
    // auth: this account's sign-in, as plugin-auth.json keeps it
    return { "acme-large": { ...provider.models["acme-large"], name: "Acme Large" } }
  },
}
```

- jianmu calls it once for each account, in that account’s scope and through its proxy. Each account serves only the models listed for it, so an account on a smaller plan isn’t sent a model it doesn’t have.
- A model is OpenCode’s `Model`: `id`, `name`;
- `api: {id, url, npm}`;
- `limit: {context, input?, output}`;
- `capabilities: {reasoning, toolcall, attachment, input: {text, image, …}}`;
- `cost: {input, output, cache: {read, write}}`;
- `variants`, `release_date`, `status`.

- `free: true`: the plan serves it at no cost to its allowance. Only this flag makes a model free, and jianmu never reads it from `rate`: set it from the vendor’s own word (its list marks the model free, or prices it at $0), not from a rate you worked out.
- `rate`: the credits a request costs, as a multiple, given as a number (`0.5`) or as the vendor writes it (`"x0.5"`). `0` reads as no rate given, not as free.
- `rateWas`: the rate before a discount that is running now.

### When the vendor can’t be reached

jianmu keeps the list it already had, as it does for a built-in subscription whose list couldn’t be fetched, when the hook does any of these:

- returns `provider.models` unchanged after a fetch that failed;
- throws;
- returns a list of its own with `list[Symbol.for("jianmu.fellBack")] = true`.

If what failed was the sign-in, throw an error with `signIn: "expired"` on it. The account is then marked as needing a new sign-in (see Sign-in state).

## Signing in

The `auth` hook is `{ provider, methods, loader, usage?, refresh?, refreshLead?, checkin?, icon?, maxConcurrency? }`. Each method is a way to sign in that the user can pick. In the app the methods are buttons; in a terminal, `jianmu plugin login <id> [<method>]` asks which one.

### An API key

```
{ type: "api", label: "Acme API key", placeholder: "acme-…" }
```

- `label` titles the key’s field. A label that only says “API key” is shown as “Acme API key”.
- `placeholder` is jianmu’s own field, a hint inside the field.
- Without an `authorize` function, the key is saved as is: `{type: "api", key, metadata?}`. Answers to `prompts` go in `metadata`.
- With `authorize(inputs)`, the plugin checks or exchanges the key itself. It returns `{type: "success", key, metadata?}` or `{type: "failed", error?}`.

### A browser or device sign-in

```
{
  type: "oauth",
  label: "Sign in with Acme",
  async authorize(inputs) {
    const d = await startDeviceCode()
    return {
      url: d.verification_uri,                    // jianmu opens it
      instructions: `Enter the code ${d.user_code}`, // and shows this
      method: "auto",                              // "auto": callback() resolves on its own
      async callback() {                           // "code": callback(code), the code the user pastes
        const t = await pollForToken(d)
        if (!t) return { type: "failed", error: "The code expired" }
        return { type: "success", refresh: t.refresh_token, access: t.access_token,
```
